Where Caiaphas the High Priest is, there are assembled the Scribes, that is, the men of the letter [marg. note: literati], who preside over the letter that killeth; and Elders, not in truth, but in the obsolete ancientness of the letter.
It follows, "Peter followed Him afar off," He would neither keep close to Him, nor altogether leave Him, but "followed afar off."

Great was the zeal of Peter, who fled not when He saw the others fly, but remained, and entered in. For though John also went in, yet he was known to the Chief Priest. He "followed afar off," because he was about to deny his Lord.
For had he kept close to his Lord"s side, he could never have denied Him. This also shews that Peter should follow his Lord"s Passion, that is, imitate it.
And also that the Church should follow, i.e. imitate, the Lord"s Passion, but with great difference. For the Church suffers for itself, but Christ for the Church.
He went in, either out of the attachment of a disciple, or natural curiosity, seeking to know what sentence the High Priest would pass, whether death, or scourging.

When the Chief Priests were thus assembled, this conventicle of ruffians sought to give their conspiracy the character of a legal trial. But it was entirely a scene of confusion and uproar, as what follows shews, "Though many false witnesses came, yet found they none."

False witnesses have place when there is any good colour for their testimony. But no pretext was found which could further their falsehoods against Jesus; notwithstanding there were many desirous to do a favour to the Chief Priests. This then is a great testimony in favour of Jesus, that He had lived and taught so irreproachably, that though they were many, and crafty, and wicked, they could find no semblance of fault in Him.

"At last came two false witnesses." How are they false witnesses, when they repeat only what we read that the Lord spoke? A false witness is one who takes what is said in a different sense from that in which it was said. Now this the Lord had spoken of the temple of His Body, and they cavil at His expressions, and by a slight change and addition produce a plausible charge. The Lord"s words were, "Destroy this temple;" [John 2:19] this they make into, I can destroy the Temple of God. He said, "Destroy," not, I will destroy, because it is unlawful to lay hands on ourselves.
Also they phrased it, "And build it again," making it apply to the temple of the Jews; but the Lord had said, "And I will raise it up again," thus clearly pointing out a living and breathing temple. For to build again, and to raise again, are two different things.
Why did they not bring forward now His breaking the Sabbath? Because He had so often confuted them on this point.

Headlong and uncontrolled rage, unable to find even a false accusation, moves the High Priest from his throne, the motion of his body shewing the emotion of his mind.
"And the High Priest arose, and said unto him, Answerest thou nothing to the things which these witness against Thee?"

He said this with a design to draw from Him some indefensible answer which might be made a snare for Him. But "Jesus held his peace," for defence had availed nothing when none would listen to it. For here was only a mockery of justice, it was in truth nothing more than the anarchy of a den of robbers.

This place teaches us to contemn the clamours of slanderers and false witnesses, and not to consider those who speak unbeseeming things of us worthy of an answer; but then, above all, when it is greater to be manfully and resolutely silent, than to plead our cause in vain.

For as God, He knew that whatever He said would be twisted into an accusation against Him. But at this His silence before false witnesses and ungodly Priests, the High Priest was exasperated, and summons Him to answer, that from any thing He says he may raise a charge against Him.

Under the Law, we do indeed find many instances of this adjuration; but I judge that a man who would live according to the Gospel should not adjure another; for if we are not permitted to swear, surely not to adjure. [marg. note: Numb 5:19, 1 Ki 22:16]
But he that regards Jesus commanding the daemons, and giving His disciples power over them, will say, that to address the daemons by the power given by the Saviour, is not to adjure them. But the High Priest did sin in laying a snare for Jesus; imitating his father, who twice asked the Saviour, "If thou be Christ the Son of God." Hence one might rightly say, that to doubt concerning the Son of God, whether Christ be He, is the work of the Devil. It was not fit that the Lord should answer the High Priest"s adjuration as though under compulsion, wherefore He neither denied nor confessed Himself to be the Son of God. For he was not worthy to be the object of Christ"s teaching, therefore He does not instruct him, but taking up his own words retorts them upon him. This sitting of the Son of Man seems to me to denote a certain regal security; by the power of God, Who is the only power, is He securely seated to Whom is given by His Father all power in heaven as in earth.
And there will come a time when the enemies shall see this establishment. Indeed this has begun to be fulfilled from the earliest time of the dispensation; for the disciples saw Him rising from the dead, and thereby saw Him seated on the right band of power.
Or, In respect of that eternity of duration which is with God, from the beginning of the world to the end of it is but one day; it is therefore no wonder that the Saviour here says, "Shortly," signifying that there is but short time before the end come. He prophesies moreover, that they should not only see Him "sitting at the right hand of power," but also "coming in the clouds of heaven." These clouds are the Prophets and Apostles, whom He commands to rain when it is required, they are the clouds that pass not away, but "bearing the image of the heavenly," [1 Cor 15:49] are worthy to be the throne of God, as "heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ." [Rom 8:17]
The same fury which drew the High Priest from his seat, impels him now to rend his clothes; for so it was customary with the Jews to do whenever they heard any blasphemy, or any thing against God.
This He did to give weight to the accusation, and to confirm by deeds what He taught in words.

And by this rending his garments, he shews that the Jews have lost the priestly glory, and that their High Priest"s throne was vacant. For by rending his garment he rent the veil of the Law which covered him.

Then, after rending his garment, he did not give sentence of himself, but asked of others, saying, "What think ye?" As was always done in undeniable cases of sin, and manifest blasphemy, and as by force driving them to a certain opinion, he anticipates the answer, "What need we any further witnesses? Behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy."
What was this blasphemy? For before He had interpreted to them as they were gathered together that text, "The Lord said unto my Lord, Sit thou on my right hand," [Matt 22:44] and they had held their peace, and had not contradicted Him. How then do they call what He now says blasphemy? "They answered and said, He is guilty of death," the same persons at once accusers, examiners, and sentencers.

How great their error! to pronounce the principle of all men"s life to be guilty of death, and not to acknowledge by the testimony of the resurrection of so many, the Fount of life, from Whom life flows to all that rise again.
As hunters who have started their game, so they exhibit a wild and drunken exultation.
"They spit in his face, and buffeted him," to fulfil the prophecy of Esaias, "I gave my cheek to the smiters, and turned not away my face from shame and spitting." [Isa 50:6]
ord.: "Prophesy unto us" is said in ridicule of His claim to be held as a Prophet by the people.
But it would have been foolish to have answered them that smote Him, and to have declared the smiter, seeing that in their madness they seem to have struck Him openly.

Observe how circumstantially the Evangelist recounts all those particulars even which seem most disgraceful, hiding or extenuating nothing, but thinking it the highest glory that the Lord of the earth should endure such things for us. This let us read continually, let us imprint in our minds, and in these things let us boast.

That, "they did spit in his face," signifies those who reject His proffered grace. They likewise buffet Him who prefer their own honour to Him; and they smite Him on the face, who, blinded with unbelief, affirm that He is not yet come, disowning and rejecting His person.

Among the other insults offered to our Lord was the threefold denial of Peter, which the several Evangelists relate in different order. Luke puts Peter"s trial first, and the ill-usage of the Lord after that; Matthew and Mark reverse the order.
"Peter sat without," that he might see the event, and not excite suspicion by any approach to Jesus.

And he, who, when he saw his Master laid hands on, drew his sword and cut off the ear, now when he sees Him enduring such insults becomes a denier, and cannot withstand the taunts of a mean servant girl.
"A damsel came unto him, saying, Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee."

What means this, that a handmaid is the first to tax him, when men would be more likely to recognise him, except that this sex might seem to sin somewhat in the Lord"s death, that they might be redeemed by His passion? "He denied before them all," because he was afraid to reveal himself; that he said, "I know not," shews that he was not yet willing to die for the Saviour.

For this reason it should seem he was permitted to waver, that the remedy of penitence might be exhibited in the head of the Church, and that none should dare to trust in his own strength, when even the blessed Peter could not escape the danger of frailty.
But not once, but twice and thrice did he deny within a short time.
We understand that having gone out after his first denial, the cock crowed the first time as Mark relates.
To shew that the sound did not keep him from denial, nor bring his promise to mind.

The second denial was not outside the door, but after he had returned to the fire; for the second maid did not see him after he had gone out, but as he was going out; his getting up to go out drew her attention, and she said to them that were there, that is, to those that were standing round the fire in the hall, "The fellow also was with Jesus of Nazareth." He who had gone out, having heard this returned, that he might by denial vindicate himself. Or, as is more likely, he did not hear what was said of him as he went out, but it was after he came back that the maid, and the other man whom Luke mentions, said to him, "And thou also art one of them."

"And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man." I know that some out of a feeling of piety towards the Apostle Peter have interpreted this place to signify that Peter denied the Man and not the God, as though he meant, "I do not know the Man, because I know the God." But the intelligent reader will see that this is trifling, for if he denied not, the Lord spoke falsely when He said, "Thou shalt deny me thrice."
[ed. note: e.g. S. Ambrose (in Luc.) says, He well denied him as man, for he knew him as God." And S. Hilary, (in loc.) "Almost without sin did he now deny the man, who had been the first to acknowledge him as Son of God; yet seeing through infirmity of the flesh, he had at least doubted, he therefore wept bitterly when he remembered that he had not been able, even after warning, to avoid the sin of that fearfulness."]
I had rather that Peter deny, than that the Lord be made out false.
In this denial of Peter we affirm that Christ is denied not only by him who denies that He is Christ, but who denies himself to be a Christian.

Let us now come to the third denial; "And after a while came they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them," (Luke"s words are, "About the space of one hour after, [Luke 22:59]) for thy speech bewrayeth thee."
Not that Peter was of a different speech or nation, but a Hebrew as his accusers were; but every province and every district has its peculiarities, and he could not disguise his native pronunciation.
Observe how baneful are communications with evil men; they even drove Peter to deny the Lord whom be had before confessed to be the Son of God.

Observe, that he said the first time, "I know not what thou sayest;" the second time, "He denied with an oath;" the third time, "He began to curse and to swear that he knew not the man." For to persevere in sinning increases sinfulness, and he who disregards light sins, falls into greater.

Spiritually; By Peter"s denial before the cock-crow , are denoted those who before Christ"s resurrection did not believe Him to be God, being perplexed by His death. In his denial after the first cock-crow, are denoted those who are in error concerning both Christ"s natures, His human and divine. By the first handmaid is signified desire; by the second, carnal delight; by them that stood by, the daemons; for by them men are led to a denial of Christ.

Or, By the first handmaid is understood the Synagogue of the Jews, which oft compelled the faithful to deny; by the second, the con greg ations of the Gentiles, who even persecuted the Christians; they that stood in the hall signify the ministers of divers heresies, who also compel men to deny the truth of Christ.
Also Peter thrice denied, because heretical error concerning Christ is limited to three kinds; they are in error respecting His divinity, His humanity, or both.

After the third denial comes the cock-crow; by which we may understand a Doctor of the Church who with chiding rouses the slumbering, saying, "Awake, ye righteous, and sin not." [1 Cor 15:14] Thus Holy Scripture uses to denote the merit of divers cases [marg. note: meritum causarum] by fixed periods, as Peter sinned at midnight and repented at cock-crow.

In another Gospel we read, that after Peter"s denial and thee cock-crow, the Saviour "looked upon Peter," [Luke 22,61] and by His look called forth those bitter tears; for it might not be that he on whom the Light of the world had looked should continue in the darkness of denial, wherefore, "he went out, and wept bitterly." For he could not do penitence sitting in Caiaphas" hall, but went forth from the assembly of the wicked, that he might wash away in bitter tears the pollution of his timid denial.

Blessed tears, O holy Apostle, which had the virtue of holy Baptism in washing off the sin of thy denial. The right hand of the Lord Jesus Christ was with thee to hold thee up before thou wast quite thrown down, and in the midst of thy perilous fall, thou receivedst strength to stand. The Rock quickly returned to its stability, recovering so great fortitude, that he who in Christ"s passion had quailed, should endure his own subsequent suffering with fearlessness and constancy.
f: COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 74

And it came to pass, after Jesus had finished all these words, that he said to his disciples.

Wishing to show that God has appointed all things in weight and number and measure, he says in a certain place to his mother: "my hour has not yet come", and again: "now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this cause I came unto this hour", and again: "Father, the hour is come; glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you" — so too he appointed the hour of the passion of his Son. Therefore, even though he frequently suffered plots from the Jews, he could suffer nothing while the devil departed from him "until a time", and he could suffer nothing until he had completed all his words which he had purposed to speak to his disciples. For this reason after he had completed all these words, then he said to his disciples. And observe that he did not say simply after he had completed all the words, but he added all these, that is, the ones he had already spoken, not those he was still going to speak. For it was still fitting that he should speak yet other words before he was handed over, and, "in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper", concerning the woman coming to him; likewise also to keep the Passover with his disciples, and to convict the betrayer lurking in hiding, and to give thanks, and to hand them the bread and the cup. It was fitting too that he foretell to his disciples that they were about to be scandalized, and to Peter that before the cock crowed he would deny three times. And still it was fitting, as the hour drew near, that he pray the more, not once nor twice but three times, until the hour should come more fully.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

"And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these sayings, He said unto His disciples, Ye know that after two days is the passover, and the Son of Man is betrayed to be crucified." In good season again doth He speak of the passion, when He had reminded them of the kingdom, and of the recompense there, and of the deathless punishment; as though He had said, Why are ye afraid at the dangers that are for a season, when such good things await you?

But mark thou, I pray thee, how He hath in all His first sayings after a new manner worked up and thrown into the shade what was most painful to them. For He said not, Ye know that after two days I am betrayed, but, "Ye know that after two days is the passover," to show that what is done is a mystery and that a feast and celebration is being kept for the salvation of the world, and that with foreknowledge He suffered all. So then, as though this were sufficient consolation for them, He did not even say anything to them now about a resurrection; for it was superfluous, after having discoursed so much about it, to speak of it again. And moreover, as I said, He shows that even His very passion is a deliverance from countless evils, having by the passover reminded them of the ancient benefits in Egypt.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 75

You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified.

If, therefore, even the hour had been determined—according to what we have said—so that he should not be handed over before all his teaching was complete, how much more had the day also been determined, on which "Christ our Passover" should be sacrificed, dissolving the Jewish Passover and handing on the new one to his disciples according to the new covenant? The month of the Passover too had to be determined; and I think the year as well, of which the prophet also spoke: "to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of salvation." He therefore foretells it to his disciples, fortifying them beforehand, so that they might not—before they had heard what was going to come about—suddenly, seeing their master handed over to the cross, be stunned with terror at the suffering befalling the Lord. For this reason he said to them: You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified. Now he does not, as some suppose, wish to say by this that after two days the day of the Passover will arrive, but that after two days the new Passover will take place. For he did not say: after two days the Passover will be or will come, so as not to point to that Passover as future which used to be kept according to the law, but the Passover will take place—that is, such as had never been made before—so that through this new Passover that ancient one might be cut away. And then he adds thus: and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified. And after two days the Passover took place, according to what had been prophesied by him: when he was handed over in the night and said to Judas as he kissed him: "Friend, for what purpose have you come?" But if after two days the Passover took place, that is on the fourteenth day of the moon, it is manifest that when he was saying these things it was, according to the Jews, the eleventh day of the moon, when he also expounded the parables mentioned above.

But by whom he was handed over is not written here. You may gather it, however, from the Scriptures, since the Father too handed him over, according to what is written: "who did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us all"; but according to other Scriptures "Judas" handed him over; yet also "Satan," who "entered into Judas," handed him over; yet also "the chief priests and the elders" "handed" him over. For this reason he here put he will be handed over impersonally, not saying by whom—which word can look to all who handed him over. But they did not all hand him over with the same purpose. For God handed him over out of mercy toward the human race, he "who did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us all." The rest, however, handed him over with a wicked purpose, each according to his own malice: Judas out of avarice, the priests out of envy, the devil out of fear, lest the human race be torn from his hand through his teaching—not noticing that the human race was more to be rescued through his death than it had been rescued through his teaching and his miracles. For he was handed over "to be crucified," so that "stripping off the principalities and powers, boldly" he might triumph over them on the wood.
Commentary on Matthew

And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples: You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified. Let those blush who think that the Savior feared death and said from dread of the passion: Father, if it can be done, let this cup pass from me. About to keep the Passover after two days, he knows that he is to be handed over to be crucified, and yet he does not avoid the snares, he does not flee in terror; so much so that, even when the others were unwilling to go, he goes on undaunted, when Thomas says: Let us go, that we too may die with him. And, wishing to put an end to the carnal festival and, as the shadow passed away, to give back the truth of the Passover, he said: With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, if only we eat it in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Moreover, as to his saying: After two days the Passover will take place, let us pass over the simple understanding and seek what is hallowed in it. After two days of the most brilliant light of the Old and the New Testament, the true Passover is celebrated for the world. The Passover (pascha), which in Hebrew is called phase, is named not from the passion, as most people think, but from the passing over, because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of the Israelites, passed over and did not strike them, or else the Lord himself, bringing help to his people, walked above them. Read the book of Exodus, of which we shall treat more fully, if life is granted to us. But our passing over, that is, phase, is celebrated in this way: if, leaving behind earthly things and Egypt, we hasten to heavenly things.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 76

Then the chief priests and the scribes and the elders of the people were gathered together into the court of the chief priest who was called Caiaphas, and they took counsel, that they might take Jesus by guile and kill him; but they said: Not on the feast day, lest perchance there be a tumult among the people.

What the prophet said—"and the princes came together into one against the Lord and against his Christ"—seems then to have been fulfilled when the chief priests and the elders of the people were gathered together into the house of the chief priest "against the Lord and against his Christ"—not true priests but priests of the people, and elders not of others but of that people which was thought to be the people of God, but was in truth the people of Gomorrah, since they said: "Crucify, crucify him", and: "Take such a one away from the earth". And what Isaiah had said: "Hear the word of the Lord, you princes of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah", fits those Jews who lay in wait, who lived in the generation of the time of Christ. And what Ezekiel says to Jerusalem: "Sodom is justified more than you", is more fittingly said to the Jerusalem over which the Lord wept than to the time of the prophet. For the princes of the people sinned worse than the men of Sodom, because, not understanding the high priest of God, they lay in wait for him; and the elders of the people, not recognizing "the firstborn of all creation" and the one older than all creatures, took counsel against him. And on account of that court (I think), in which they took counsel that they might take Jesus by guile, Jerusalem was made desolate. For it was fitting that there should no longer be a city that had acted against the founder of the whole world—a city which earlier indeed had killed "the prophets", but afterward the Lord of the prophets.

That they might take him by guile. Therefore fittingly the prophet said concerning them: "May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips". And they wished to take him by guile and to kill him, lest there be a tumult among that people which had seen Jesus doing many signs and wonders. And on this account many indeed of these were for him, who perhaps had said that "a great prophet has risen up in Israel"; but others were against him, who had said: "This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul the prince of demons". It was necessary, therefore, that a tumult arise when the Lord was seized, on account of the differing dispositions of the people—some loving Christ and some hating him, some believing and some not believing. For their counsel stood as though firm (although those very men who took counsel were not to stand), that he should be killed not on the feast day but on another day; namely, so that "Christ our passover" might be sacrificed, that, leaving behind the unleavened bread of the Jews, we might keep festival in the spiritual and true unleavened bread. But consider, if you can, that every word which in any way professes the doctrine of God is said to be a prince of the priests of God. But since there are many words of false teachings, as though priests of God, yet not of God but of the people that has been led astray by them, they take counsel against the one and true word of God. Yet the word of God offers itself indeed to those who lie in wait, and nonetheless rises again, unchanged and uncorrupted by them, and ascends into heaven, that it may receive those who take up their cross and follow him.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

"Then were assembled together the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders of the people, in the palace of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and consulted that they might take Jesus by subtlety, and kill Him. But they said, Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people."

Seest thou the unspeakable corruption of the Jewish state? Attempting unlawful acts, they come to the high priest, desiring to obtain their authority from that quarter, whence they ought to have found hindrance.

And how many high priests were there? For the law wills there should be one, but then there were many. Whence it is manifest, that the Jewish constitution had begun to dissolve. For Moses, as I said, commanded there should be one, and that when he was dead there should be another, and by the life of this person He measured the banishment of them that had involuntarily committed manslaughter. How then were there at that time many high priests? They were afterwards made for a year. And this the evangelist declared, when he was speaking of Zacharias, saying, that he was of the course of Abia. Those therefore doth he here call high priests, who had been high priests.
Commentary on Matthew

Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the court of the chief priest, who was called Caiaphas; and they took counsel to seize Jesus by guile and kill him. Those who, with the Passover near, ought to have been preparing the victims, polishing the walls of the temple, sweeping the pavements, cleaning the vessels, and purifying themselves according to the rite of the law, so that they might become worthy to eat the lamb, gather together and enter into counsel how they may kill the Lord: not fearing sedition, as the simple wording shows, but taking care lest he be taken out of their hands by the help of the people.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

What did they consult together? That they might seize Him secretly, or that they might put Him to death? Both; for they feared the people. Wherefore also they waited for the feast to be past; for "they said, Not on the feast day." For the devil, lest he should make the passion conspicuous, was not willing it should take place at the passover; but they, lest there should be an uproar. Mark them then ever fearing, not the ills from God, neither lest any greater pollution should arise to them from the season, but in every case the ills from men.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 79

Yet for all this, boiling with anger, they changed their purpose again. For though they had said, "Not at the feast time;" when they found the traitor, they waited not for the time, but slew Him at the feast. But why did they take Him then? They were boiling with rage, as I said; and they expected then to find Him, and all things they did as blinded. For though He Himself made the greatest use of their wickedness for His own dispensation, they were not surely for this guiltless, but deserving of inflictions without number for their temper of mind. At least when all should be set free, even the guilty, then these men slew the guiltless, Him that had conferred on them countless benefits, and who for a time had neglected the Gentiles for their sake.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 77

When Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, there came to him a woman having an alabaster jar of precious ointment and poured it upon his head as he reclined. But when his disciples saw it, they were indignant, and so forth (26:6—13).

Many indeed suppose that the four evangelists have given an account of one and the same woman, because they wrote something of this kind about a woman and all alike named an alabaster jar of ointment; but John, instead of the alabaster jar, put "a pound of ointment." But also what is said, this could have been sold and given to the poor, was said by Matthew and Mark and John; and that Christ declared that ointment to have been poured out for his burial, these too expounded; and that it happened in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, these three wrote; but John indeed said Bethany, where "they made him a supper and Martha was serving and Lazarus was one of those reclining, and Mary took a pound of ointment of pure precious nard" and so forth, from which it appears that they made a supper for him. But Luke, although he did not put Simon as a leper, nevertheless said that he was a Pharisee, who had asked Jesus "to eat with him," just as the Lord himself testifies concerning his name, saying to him there: "Simon, Simon, I have something to say to you." There seems, therefore, to be much similarity and a certain kinship concerning the woman among the four evangelists.

Yet I will say to those who think that it was one woman about whom all the evangelists wrote: Do you suppose that this woman who poured upon the head of Jesus the precious ointment, as Matthew and Mark expounded, is the same one who also "anointed his feet with myrrh," as Luke and John expounded? But it is not possible that the evangelists, in expounding about the same woman — since they were "perfected in the same understanding and in the same spirit and in the same judgment," they who were to minister the salvation of the churches — should have said things contrary to one another. But if anyone thinks that she was the one who anointed the Lord's feet with ointment in Luke and John, let him tell us whether Mary here was the very one who in Luke is written to have been "a sinner in the city," who "learning that he had reclined in the house of the Pharisee brought an alabaster jar of ointment and standing behind at his feet weeping began to wash his feet with her tears." For it is not credible that Mary whom "Jesus loved," the sister of Martha "who had chosen the better part," should be said to have been "a sinner in the city." And do you suppose that the woman who according to Matthew and Mark poured upon the head of Jesus the precious ointment is not written to have been a sinner, whereas the one who according to Luke is reported as "a sinner" did not dare to come to the head of Christ but "washed his feet with her tears" as though scarcely even worthy of his very feet, from sadness working "repentance unto stable salvation"? And the one who is in Luke weeps and sheds many tears, so as to wash the "feet" of Jesus "with her tears," whereas the one who in John is Mary is introduced neither as a sinner nor as weeping. Perhaps then someone will say that there were four women about whom the evangelists wrote; but I rather agree that there were three: one indeed about whom Matthew and Mark wrote, making no difference in their exposition in that chapter; another about whom Luke wrote; and yet another about whom John wrote, since she differs from the other women not only in the things which are written about the ointment, but because "Jesus loved" Mary and Martha — although she too is reported to have been in Bethany, just as also the woman about whom Matthew and Mark expound. There is a third difference. For Matthew indeed and Mark expound that this happened in the house of Simon the leper; but John says that "Jesus six days before the Passover came into Bethany, where Lazarus was whom Jesus had raised, and they made him a supper" — not Simon, but Mary and Martha, perhaps also Lazarus, "and Martha was serving, but Lazarus was one of those reclining." Furthermore, according to John, "six days before the Passover he came into Bethany," when also Mary and Martha "made him a supper"; but here, when also, as he reclined in the house of Simon the leper, there came to him a woman, "after two days it was to be the Passover," as was said above. It remains that someone may say: If Matthew and Mark wrote about one woman, but John about another, and Luke indeed about a third, how is it that the disciples, once rebuked by Christ in the case of one woman (as being wrongly indignant about the woman's deed), did not correct themselves, so as not to be indignant over another woman doing likewise? Therefore let him know that in Matthew and Mark the disciples are indignant out of a good intention, but in John Judas alone out of a desire to steal, whereas in Luke no one murmurs. From these things, then, and others which you yourself will be able to observe, it is certain that either the evangelists say things contrary to one another, so that some of them even lie, or (if it is impious to believe this) it is necessary to say that the evangelists did not all write about the same woman, but either about three or about four. But someone a little bolder will say: Perhaps according to the history there was some one woman who did something of this kind — suppose too a second (if you wish) and a third — yet the evangelists' chief purpose was directed toward the mysteries, and they were not much concerned to narrate according to the truth of the history, but to expound the mysteries of things which arose out of the history. For which reason they also wove in certain discourses fitting and consonant with the understandings of the mysteries.

But concerning these things, which are expounded among the four evangelists on account of the women or of the one woman (as many suppose), we have treated more carefully in expounding the Gospel according to John — those things which seemed to us, since they were similar and kindred yet as it were contrary and divergent. But now let us touch on them briefly. Reasonably, then, Luke, when he spoke of the sinful woman, introduced her weeping more abundantly, so as even to wash the feet of Jesus, and indeed not pouring on the ointment but only anointing, and not the head but the feet. But that woman, who was not accused as a sinner, did not anoint but poured out, and not upon the feet, but upon the head. But if anyone should also treat of the things written about Mary the sister of Lazarus, who likewise "anointed" the Lord's "feet," let him note for himself what is written there, that the whole "house was filled with the odor of the ointment"; which is not written of her who was said to be "a sinner," but neither about the woman of whom Matthew and Mark wrote, who was not said to have been "a sinner," is anything of this kind written, that the whole "house was filled with the odor of the ointment."

Perhaps then through the differences of these women the differences of the faithful are demonstrated, of whom some indeed pour upon the head of Jesus the precious ointment, but others anoint not the head, but the feet, while others do not pour on abundantly, but only anoint; and of those anointing, some indeed anoint with such ointment that the whole house is filled with the odor of his very divinity, while others anoint not with such indeed, yet with one likewise acceptable to Christ, since they too anoint his feet with ointment — feet which the Pharisee did not anoint even with "oil." And it was fitting that these things be done in Bethany, which is interpreted HOUSE OF OBEDIENCE, and by this woman who poured out the ointment upon the head of the Lord, not accused as "a sinner in the city," and by Mary, at whose house, when a banquet was made for Jesus, she came to him and anointed. But that the house of obedience should be understood as the Church, no one doubts. But she who in Luke was called "a sinner" was not yet worthy to be in Bethany, although she was doing penance for her sins. For she still had the less, so that afterward she might be found made in the house of obedience (as now perfected) and be called neither "a sinner" nor "weeping" and washing the Lord's "feet," but herself too pouring the ointment upon his head. But Simon too is a mystery of OBEDIENCE, since so it is interpreted, but the obedience of the letter, not of the spirit: for which reason Simon, lifted up from the letter of the law through Jesus to the spiritual law, was no longer Simon only, but was made also Peter, and in place of the Jewish edifice was held worthy of the edifice of the Church to be founded upon the rock. Jesus therefore came to be in the house of Simon indeed, of one OBEDIENT, yet a leper and still having need of cleansing from Jesus. But it was not mentioned in Luke concerning Simon that he was also a leper; I judge that he himself was a debtor of fifty denarii and had already received remission of them, because he had loved little; yet loving somewhat, "he asked him to eat with him." But there came a woman (not a sinner) according to Matthew and Mark, having an alabaster jar of precious ointment. And consider how carefully among these, who did not report a sinner, her ointment is praised as precious. But in Luke, who expounded the sinful woman, the ointment is simply named, neither precious nor "of pure nard," such that "the house" might be filled "from the odor" of it; for she could not yet have ointments of this kind, but this was a great thing, that she could anoint the Lord's feet even with "ointment." But of this woman the ointment is reported as precious, for it was not fitting that what was poured out upon the head of the Savior should be not precious.

And over the ointment indeed of the sinful woman, anointing the Lord's feet and not pouring out, neither were the disciples indignant nor did they grieve, nor did Judas say: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" But over the woman in Matthew and Mark the disciples were indignant and grieved at the loss of the ointment which was running down from his head to the rest of his body. For even if that ointment could have been sold for a great price and given to the poor, nevertheless this ought not to have been done, because it was fitting that it be poured upon the head of Christ with a holy and seemly pouring. But those who strive to understand these things according to the simple text, let them say what beauty the ointment poured upon the head of Jesus praiseworthily had according to the text, that it should be poured upon the head of such and so great a master. That ointment therefore was not worthy of the poor nor fitting (as regards its own honor) that it be divided among many, but that, remaining whole, it should be poured upon the head of Jesus only. For which reason Jesus also receives the woman who had done this, and says to the indignant disciples: "Let her be, and do not be troublesome to her, for she has worked a good work in me." And to such a degree is the praise of a good work of this kind effective, that it exhorts all of us to fill the Lord's head with fragrant and rich works, so that of us too it may be said that we have done a good work upon his head; for we always indeed have (as long as we remain in this life) the poor with us and having need of care from those who have advanced in the word and have been made rich in the wisdom of God, but they cannot suffice to have always, by days and nights, with them the Son of God, the Word of God and the Wisdom and all things, whatever our Lord the Savior is.

See also what he says: she has worked a good work in me, since he did not say concerning the sinful woman anointing his feet that "she did a good work in me." But if it is also necessary to discuss what he says, she has done it to prepare me for burial, you will compare with it what is said: "we were buried together with Christ through baptism, and we rose again together with him." Consider furthermore that concerning the woman according to Luke it is not said, amen I say to you: wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she did shall be told in memory of her, but concerning the woman according to Matthew and Mark this is written. For it was just, not concerning her who had anointed the feet, but concerning this one who had poured the ointment upon the head of Jesus, that it should be said, wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, that also which she did shall be told in memory of her. If, then, we wish that of us too it may be said what we do to Jesus, pouring the precious ointment upon his head, let us advance from the anointing of his feet to pouring the precious ointment upon his head.

But what oil is and what ointment, and what ointment is that which serves for anointing the body of Christ and what for the head, is difficult indeed to explain. Nevertheless we shall attempt to show that which seems to us, knowing most certainly that oil everywhere in the scriptures is understood either as a work of mercy (by which the lamp of the word, being nourished, shines brightly) or as doctrine (by whose constant hearing the word of faith which is kindled in us is nourished and shines more brightly). Just as, then, generally everything with which one is anointed is called oil, but of oil one kind is ointment another kind is not ointment, likewise of ointment one kind is a middling ointment, another precious: so every just act is called a good work, but of a good work one kind is what we do for the sake of men or according to men, and another what is for the sake of God and according to God. Likewise this very thing, which we do for the sake of God, one kind is what serves the use of men, and another what does not serve the use of men but only the glory of God. For instance, someone does good to a man, moved by natural justice, not for the sake of God (as sometimes the Gentiles too did and as many men do), that work is common oil of no great odor, and yet it too is acceptable to God; as Daniel signifies, saying to Nebuchadnezzar, who did not know God: hear my counsel, O king, and redeem your sins with almsgivings. Something of this kind Peter too says in Clement, that the good works which are done by unbelievers in this world profit them, but not also in that world for the attaining of eternal life; and fittingly, because they too do not do them for the sake of God, but for the sake of human nature itself. But those who do them for the sake of God, that is, the faithful, it profits them not only in this world, but also in that, and rather in that.

But what the faithful do for the sake of God, this is the ointment of good odor. But this very work of the faithful for the sake of God, which is ointment, one kind is done for the benefit of men — for instance almsgivings, visitations of the sick, receptions of strangers, humility, meekness, forbearance, and other things of this kind which profit men. He who does these things toward Christians anoints the Lord's feet with ointment, because they are the Lord's feet, with which he always walks. This the penitent are especially wont to do for the remission of their sins, and that is the work which is called ointment, fragrant indeed, but not the highest. But he who is zealous for chastity, perseveres in fastings and prayers, has patience in adversities like Job, in temptations does not fear to confess the truth of God (all which things profit other men nothing, but serve only the glory of God), this is the ointment which anoints both the head of the Lord, Christ, and from there runs through the whole body of Christ, that is, through the whole Church; and this is the ointment exceedingly precious from whose odor the whole house is filled, that is, the Church of Christ; and this is the work proper not to the penitent, but to the perfect saints. Or certainly: the doctrine which is necessary to men, through which are nourished souls poor in spiritual goods or perhaps also weak in sins, this is the middling ointment with which the Lord's feet are anointed; but the knowledge of the true faith which pertains to God alone is the precious ointment with which is anointed the head of Christ, God.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 80

This woman seems indeed to be one and the same with all the evangelists, yet she is not so; but though with the three she doth seem to me to be one and the same, yet not so with John, but another person, one much to be admired, the sister of Lazarus.

But not without purpose did the evangelist mention the leprosy of Simon, but in order that He might show whence the woman took confidence, and came unto Him. For inasmuch as the leprosy seemed a most unclean disease, and to be abhorred, and yet she saw Jesus had both healed the man (for else He would not have chosen to have tarried with a leper), and had gone into his house; she grew confident, that He would also easily wipe off the uncleanness of her soul. And not for nought doth He name the city also, Bethany, but that thou mightest learn, that of His own will He cometh to His passion. For He who before this was fleeing through the midst of them; then, at the time when their envy was most kindled, comes near within about fifteen furlongs; so completely was His former withdrawing Himself a part of a dispensation.

The woman therefore having seen Him, and having taken confidence from thence came unto Him. For if she that had the issue of blood, although conscious to herself of nothing like this, yet because of that natural seeming uncleanness, approached Him trembling and in fear; much more was it likely this woman should be slow, and shrink back because of her evil conscience. Wherefore also it is after many women, the Samaritan, the Canaanite, her that had the issue of blood, and other besides, that she cometh unto Him, being conscious to herself of much impurity; and then not publicly but in a house. And whereas all the others were coming unto Him for the healing of the body alone, she came unto Him by way of honor only, and for the amendment of the soul. For neither was she at all afflicted in body, so that for this most especially one might marvel at her.

And not as to a mere man did she come unto Him; for then she would not have wiped His feet with her hair, but as to one greater than man can be. Therefore that which is the most honorable member of the whole body, this she laid at Christ's feet, even her own head.
Commentary on Matthew

Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. About to suffer for the whole world and to redeem all the nations by his blood, he stays in Bethany, the house of obedience, which once was the house of Simon the leper: not that he still remained a leper at that time, but he who had been a leper before was afterwards cleansed by the Savior, the former name remaining so that the power of the one who healed might appear. For in the catalogue of the apostles too Matthew is called the tax collector, with his former fault and occupation, though he had certainly ceased to be a tax collector. Some want the house of Simon the leper to be understood as that part of the people which believed in the Lord and was healed by him. Simon himself, too, is said to mean obedient; according to another understanding he can be interpreted as pure, and in his house the Church was healed.
A Treatise on the Soul

We may not, I say, we may not call into question the truth of the (poor vilified) senses, lest we should even in Christ Himself, bring doubt upon the truth of their sensation; lest perchance it should be said that He did not really "behold Satan as lightning fall from heaven; " that He did not really hear the Father's voice testifying of Himself; or that He was deceived in touching Peter's wife's mother; or that the fragrance of the ointment which He afterwards smelled was different from that which He accepted for His burial; and that the taste of the wine was different from that which He consecrated in memory of His blood.
HOMILIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS, HOMILY 1

In the Gospel too a woman, taking an alabaster jar of ointment of costly spikenard, poured it over the head and feet of Jesus. Observe diligently what the two women poured over the head of the Savior. For the sinful woman is shown to have poured over his feet, and she who is not called a sinner over his head. Observe, I say, and you will find, in the Gospel reading, that not fables and tales were written by the Evangelists, but mysteries. And so the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment — if what the sinful woman had is to be referred to the feet, and what the woman who was no sinner had, to the head. Nor is it any wonder that the house was filled with the fragrance, since this world has been filled with it. In the same place it is written of Simon the leper and his house. I think that the leper, the prince of this world, is also called "Simon the leper," whose house at the coming of Christ was filled with sweet fragrance, when the sinful woman did penance, and the holy woman drenched the head of Jesus with the fragrances of the ointment.
Commentary on Matthew

A woman came to him having an alabaster of precious ointment, and she poured it over his head as he reclined. Let no one think that she who poured ointment over the head is the same as she who poured it over the feet. For the latter both washes with tears and wipes with her hair and is openly called a harlot, whereas of this one nothing of the kind is written. Nor indeed could a harlot at once become worthy of the Lord's head. Another evangelist, in place of the alabaster of precious ointment (which is a kind of marble), put pistic nard, that is, true and without guile, to show the faith of the Church and of the Gentiles.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 80

And whence had they this thought? They used to hear their Master saying, "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice," and blaming the Jews, because they omitted the weightier matters, judgment, and mercy, and faith, and discoursing much on the mount concerning almsgiving, and from these things they inferred with themselves, and reasoned, that if He accepts not whole burnt offerings, neither the ancient worship, much more will He not accept the anointing of oil.
Commentary on Matthew

But the disciples, seeing it, were indignant, saying: To what purpose is this waste? For this could have been sold for much and given to the poor. I know that some cavil at this passage, asking why another evangelist said that Judas alone was saddened, because he held the purse and had been a thief from the beginning, while Matthew writes that all the apostles were indignant; they do not know the figure that is called σύλληψις (syllepsis), by which all are customarily named for one and one for many. For Paul the apostle too, in his letter which is written to the Hebrews (although many of the Latins have doubts about it), when he had described the sufferings and merits of the saints, added: They were stoned, they were tempted, they were sawn asunder, they died by the slaughter of the sword, though the Jews hold that only one, the prophet Isaiah, was sawn. We can also say otherwise: that the apostles were truly indignant on account of the poor, but Judas on account of his own gain. Hence his muttering too is set down together with a charge: that he had no care for the poor but wished to provide for his own theft.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 50

Why then doth He Himself say, "The poor always ye have with you, but me ye have not always?" Why, for this reason most of all should we give alms, that we have Him not always an hungered, but in the present life only. But if thou art desirous to learn also the whole meaning of the saying, understand that this was said not with a view to His disciples, although it seem so, but to the woman's weakness. That is, her disposition being still rather imperfect, and they doubting about her; to revive her He said these things. For in proof that for her comfort He said it, He added, "Why trouble ye the woman?" And with regard to our having Him really always with us, He saith, "Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." From all which it is evident, that for no other object was this said, but that the rebuke of the disciples might not wither the faith of the woman, just then budding.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 80

But though they thus thought, He knowing her intention suffers her. For indeed great was her reverence, and unspeakable her zeal; wherefore of this exceeding condescension, He permitted the oil to be poured even on His head.

For if He refused not to become man, and to be borne in the womb, and to be fed at the breast, why marvellest thou, if He doth not utterly reject this? For like as the Father suffered a savor of meat, and smoke, even so did He the harlot, accepting, as I have already said, her intention. For Jacob too anointed a pillar to God, and oil was offered in the sacrifices, and the priests were anointed with ointment.

But the disciples not knowing her purpose found fault unseasonably, and by the things they laid to her charge, they show the woman's munificence. For saying, that it might have been sold for three hundred pence, they showed how much this woman had spent on the ointment, and how great generosity she had manifested. Wherefore He also rebuked them, saying, "Why trouble ye the woman?" And He adds a reason, as it was His will again to put them in mind of His passion, "For she did it," He said, "for my burial." And another reason. "For ye have the poor always with you, but me ye have not always;" and, "Wheresoever the gospel shall be preached, that shall be told also which this woman hath done."

Seest thou how again He declares beforehand the going forth unto the Gentiles, in this way also consoling them for His death, if after the cross His power was so to shine forth, that the Gospel should be spread abroad in every part of the earth.

Who then is so wretched as to set his face against so much truth? For lo! what He said is come to pass, and to whatever part of the earth thou mayest go, thou wilt see her celebrated.

And yet neither was the person that did it distinguished, nor had what was done many witnesses, neither was it in a theatre, but in a house, that it took place, the disciples only being present.

Who then proclaimed it, and caused it to be spread abroad? It was the power of Him who is speaking these words. And while of countless kings and generals the noble exploits even of those whose memorials remain have sunk into silence; and having overthrown cities, and encompassed them with walls, and set up trophies, and enslaved many nations, they are not known so much as by hearsay, nor by name, though they have both set up statues, and established laws; yet that a woman who was a harlot poured out oil in the house of some leper, in the presence of ten men, this all men celebrate throughout the world; and so great a time has passed, and yet the memory of that which was done hath not faded away, but alike Persians and Indians, Scythians and Thracians, and Sarmatians, and the race of the Moors, and they that dwell in the British Islands, spread abroad that which was done secretly in a house by a woman that had been a harlot.

Great is the loving-kindness of the Lord. He endureth an harlot, an harlot kissing his feet, and moistening them with oil, and wiping them with her hair, and He receives her, and reproves them that blame her. For neither was it right that for so much zeal the woman should be driven to despair.

But mark thou this too, how far they were now raised up above the world, and forward in almsgiving. And why was it He did not merely say, "She hath wrought a good work," but before this, "Why trouble ye the woman?" That they might learn not at the beginning to require too high principles of the weaker sort. Therefore neither doth He examine the act merely itself by itself, but taking into account the person of the woman. And indeed if He had been making a law, He would not have brought in the woman, but that thou mightest learn that for her sake these things were said, that they might not mar her budding faith, but rather cherish it, therefore He saith it, teaching us whatever good thing may be done by any man, though it be not quite perfect, to receive it, and encourage it, and advance it, and not to seek all perfection at the beginning. For, that at least He Himself would rather have desired this, is manifest from the fact, that He required a bag to be borne, who had not where to lay His head. But then the time demanded not this, that He should correct the deed, but that He should accept it only. For even as, if any one asked Him, without the woman's having done it, He would not have approved this; so, after she had done it, He looks to one thing only, that she be not driven to perplexity by the reproof of the disciples, but that she should go from His care, having been made more cheerful and better. For indeed after the oil had been poured out, their rebuke had no seasonableness.

Do thou then likewise, if thou shouldest see any one provide sacred vessels and offer them, and loving to labor upon any other ornament of the church, about its walls or floor; do not command what has been made to be sold, or overthrown, lest thou spoil his zeal. But if, before he had provided them, he were to tell thee of it, command it to be given to the poor; forasmuch as He also did this not to spoil the spirit of the woman, and as many things as He says, He speaks for her comfort.

Then because He had said, "She hath done it for my burial;" that He might not seem to perplex the woman, by making mention of such a thing as this, His burial and death, I mean; see how by that which follows He recovers her, saying, "What she hath done shall be spoken of in the whole world."

And this was at once consolation to His disciples, and comfort and praise to her. For all men, He saith, shall celebrate her hereafter; and now too hath she announced beforehand my passion, by bringing unto me what was needed for a funeral, let not therefore any man reprove her. For I am so far from condemning her as having done amiss, or from blaming her as having not acted rightly, that I will not suffer what hath been done to lie hid, but the world shall know that which has been done in a house, and in secret. For in truth the deed came of a reverential mind, and fervent faith, and a contrite soul.

And wherefore did He promise the woman nothing spiritual; but the perpetual memory? From this He is causing her to feel a confidence about the other things also. For if she hath wrought a good work, it is quite evident she shall receive a due reward.
Commentary on Matthew

But Jesus, knowing it, said to them: Why do you trouble the woman? She has wrought a good work on me; for you always have the poor with you, but me you will not always have. Another question arises: why the Lord said to the disciples after the resurrection: Behold, I am with you even to the consummation of the world, and now says: but me you will not always have. But it seems to me that in this place he speaks of his bodily presence: that after the resurrection he would by no means be with them in such a way as he is now, in all shared life and familiarity. Mindful of this, the Apostle says: And if we had known Jesus Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer.
Commentary on Matthew

For in putting this ointment on my body, she has done it for my burial. What you think to be a waste of ointment is the office of burial. Nor is it strange if she has given me the good odor of her faith, since I am going to pour out my blood for her.
Commentary on Matthew

Amen I say to you: Wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, what she has done shall also be told in memory of her. In the whole world it is not so much this woman as the Church that is proclaimed, because she buried the Savior, because she anointed his head. And note his knowledge of things to come: that, about to suffer after two days and to die, he knows that his Gospel is to be celebrated in all the world.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 78

Then one of the twelve, who is called Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said to them: What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you? But they set for him thirty pieces of silver, and from then on he was seeking an opportunity to hand him over to them.

Judas is interpreted CONFESSOR. Since, therefore, there are two disciples of Christ named by this name, inasmuch as Luke the evangelist counts among the twelve apostles that there were "Judas of James and Judas Iscariot," and since nothing with Christ is empty of a mystery, I judge that these two Judases were, in a mystery, figures of the Christians who confess the faith of Christ. Of these, one part indeed remains faithfully with Christ, whose mystery was Judas of James. But the other part, after it has believed and confessed the faith of Christ, on account of avarice forsakes Christ and, having become a betrayer of the very truth, passes over to heresies and to the false priests of the false Jews—that is, of pretended Christians—and hands over to them Christ (so far as it is in its power), that is, "the word of truth," so that the word of truth may be crucified and killed by them; whose mystery was Judas Iscariot, who went to the priests and bargained for a price for the betrayal of Christ. I have heard someone expounding that the homeland of the traitor Judas is called, according to the Hebrew interpretation, THE STRANGLED. And if this is so, a great fittingness is found between the name of his homeland and the manner of his own death, since he too, hanging himself with a noose, being strangled, fulfilled the prophecy of the name of his homeland. This Judas, then, to whom it was said through the prophet: "But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance," fell, though he had been one of those whom Christ took up for the leadership of the Christian people. And see how that which is written, "But you shall die like men, and you shall fall like one of the princes," is referred now to that prince who fell "like lightning from heaven," now to Judas, who, chosen to the princedom of the apostolate and, as it were, established in heaven, and himself, as it were, set beforehand like lightning, fell, going into the ruin of betrayal (against the one chief of the priests, who had been made "forever" a "priest according to the order of Melchizedek") to many chief priests and adversaries of the one high priest, that he might sell for a price him who willed to redeem the whole world from the curse of the law and of all sin, and to redeem us "not with corruptible" money, "but with his own precious blood."

But let us hear what Judas said to the priests: What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you? For he wished to receive money and to hand over the word of God, which all do who receive some bodily or worldly thing, that they may hand over and cast out from their soul the Savior and the word of truth which was in them. And you may fittingly use this example against all who, committing any sin whatsoever, on account of avarice and for the sake of money or of some gain, despise the word of God and, as it were, hand it over. For men of this kind seem, as it were, openly to cry out and to say to the adversary powers that furnish some gain for the sin of transgressing the word of God: What are you willing to give me, and I will hand him over to you? And even though he be handed over, it happens indeed outside of the one who hands him over: but overcoming those who seem to have received him, he works things befitting himself, so that those desiring to make him void accomplish nothing against him. But they appointed to give him thirty pieces of silver, appointing for him a giving as great as the number of years the Savior had sojourned in this world. For at thirty years of age, having been baptized, he began to preach the Gospel, having become as it were like Joseph at thirty years of age, that he might distribute grain to his brothers. For just as then that grain had been prepared by God for the sons of Israel, yet was distributed also to the Egyptians, so the Gospel had indeed been prepared for the saints, yet was preached also to the unbelieving and the unrighteous.

From then on he was seeking an opportunity to hand him over. But what sort of opportunity Judas was seeking, Luke has explained more plainly, saying: "And he was seeking an opportunity to hand him over to them without the crowd," that is, when the people was not about him, but he was apart with his disciples. And this he did, handing him over after the supper, when he was apart in the estate of Gethsemane; for Judas reckoned that the opportunity was his after the bargain which he made, when Jesus was not with the multitude. And see whether even until now this opportunity does not seem the same to the betrayers of the word of truth, who wish to betray Christ, God the Word, in the time of the persecution of Christians, when the multitude of believers is not about the word of truth and cannot hinder or restrain the persecutors, especially where few of the faithful are to be found. And since there is a time for all things, Solomon saying: "a time to give birth, and a time to die," and the rest, this is the time proper to the betrayers of the word of truth, when there are not many faithful about Christ.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 80

"Then went one of the twelve, he that was called Judas Iscariot, unto the chief priests, and said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver Him unto you?" Then. When? When these things were spoken, when He had said, it is for my burial, and not even thereby was he moved to compunction, neither when he heard that the Gospel should be preached everywhere did he fear (and yet it was the language of unspeakable power), but when women showed so much honor, and women that had been harlots, then he wrought the devil's works.

But what can be the reason they mention his surname? Because there was also another Judas. And they do not shrink from saying, He was of the twelve; so entirely do they hide none of those things which seem to be matters of reproach. And yet they might have said merely this, that he was one of the disciples, for there were others besides. But now they add, of the twelve, as though they had said, of the first company of those selected as the best, of them with Peter and John. Because for one thing did they care, for truth alone, not for concealing what things were done.

For this cause many of the signs they pass by, but of the things that appear to be matters of reproach they conceal nothing; but though it be word, though it be deed, though it be what you will of this kind, they proclaim it with confidence.

And not these only, but even John himself, who utters the higher doctrines. For he most of all tells us of the affronts and the reproachful things that were done unto Him.

And see how great is the wickedness of Judas, in that he comes unto them of his own accord, in that he does this for money, and for such a sum of money.

But Luke saith, that he conferred with the chief captains. For after that the Jews became seditious, the Romans set over them those that should provide for their good order. For their government had now undergone a change according to the prophecy.

To these then he went and said, "What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you. And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver. And from that time he sought opportunity to betray Him." For indeed he was afraid of the multitude, and desired to seize him alone.

Oh madness! how did covetousness altogether blind him! For he that had often seen Him when He went through the midst, and was not seized, and when He afforded many demonstrations of His Godhead and power, looked to lay hold on Him; and this while He was using like a charm for him so many, both awful and soothing words, to put an end to this evil thought. For not even at the supper did He forbear from this care of him, but unto the last day discoursed to him of these things. But he profited nothing. Yet not for that did the Lord cease to do His part. Knowing this, then, let us also not intermit to do all things unto them that sin and are remiss, warning, teaching, exhorting, admonishing, advising, though we profit nothing. For Christ indeed foreknew that the traitor was incorrigible, yet nevertheless He ceased not to supply what could be done by Himself, as well admonishing as threatening and bewailing over him, and nowhere plainly, nor openly, but in a concealed way. And at the very time of the betrayal, He allowed him even to kiss Him, but this benefited him nothing. So great an evil is covetousness, this made him both a traitor, and a sacrilegious robber.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

For what would the madman do like this? He poured not forth foam out of his mouth, but he poured forth the murder of his Lord. He distorted not his hands, but stretched them out for the price of precious blood. Wherefore his madness was greater, because he was mad being in health.

But he doth not utter, sayest thou, sounds without meaning. And what is more without meaning than this language, "What will ye give me, and I will deliver Him unto you?" "I will deliver," the devil spake by that mouth. But he did not smite the ground with his feet struggling? Nay, how much better so to struggle, than thus to stand upright. But sayest thou, he did not cut himself with stones? Yet how much better, than to do such things as these!
Commentary on Matthew

And he said to them: What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you? But they fixed for him thirty pieces of silver. Unhappy Judas! The loss which he believed he had suffered from the pouring out of the ointment he wishes to make good with the price of his master. And yet he does not demand a fixed sum, so that the betrayal might at least seem profitable, but, as though handing over a cheap slave, he left it in the power of the buyers to give as much as they wished. Who fixed for him thirty pieces of silver. Joseph was not sold, as many think, for twenty pieces of gold, according to the LXX translators, but, according to the Hebrew truth, for twenty pieces of silver. For the servant could not be more precious than the master.
An Answer to the Jews

For that you would do thus at the beginning of the first month of your new (years) even Moses prophesied, when he was foretelling that all the community of the sons of lsrµl was to immolate at eventide a lamb, and were to eat this solemn sacrifice of this day (that is, of the passover of unleavened bread) with bitterness; "and added that "it was the passover of the Lord," that is, the passion of Christ. Which prediction was thus also fulfilled, that "on the first day of unleavened bread" you slew Christ; and (that the prophecies might be fulfilled) the day hasted to make an "eventide,"-that is, to cause darkness, which was made at mid-day; and thus "your festive days God converted into grief, and your canticles into lamentation.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 79

Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him: Where do you wish that we prepare for you to eat the Passover? And Jesus said: Go into the city to a certain man, and say to him, and so forth.

But in Mark he speaks thus: "And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover was being sacrificed, his disciples say to him: Where do you wish that we go and prepare for you to eat the Passover? And he sent two of his disciples, saying: Go into the city, and as you enter a man will meet you carrying a jar of water; and wherever he enters, say to the householder: The Master says: Where is my guest-chamber, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples? And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and prepared; there prepare for us".

As therefore it appears, it was one and the same day of the Passover, when it was fitting to sacrifice the Passover, and of Unleavened Bread, when it was fitting to remove the "old leaven" and to eat unleavened bread with the flesh of the lamb. And the day of the Passover indeed was one, but of Unleavened Bread seven, the day of the Passover being of course counted together with the other six. In accordance with these things perhaps some one of the untaught, falling into Ebionism, will inquire (from the fact that Jesus celebrated the Passover after the Jewish manner corporally, as also the first day of Unleavened Bread and the Passover), saying that it is fitting that we too, as imitators of Christ, do likewise; not considering that Jesus, "when the fullness of time had come" and he had been sent, was made "of a woman", was "made" "under the law", not that he might leave those who were under the law under the law, but that he might lead them out from the law. If therefore he came for this reason, that he might lead out those who were under the law, how much more is it not fitting that those enter into the law who before had been outside the law?

Therefore we indeed go out from the letter of the law, but being established beneath the spiritual power of the law, celebrating spiritually we fulfill all things that there are commanded to be celebrated corporally. For we cast out the "old leaven" of "malice and wickedness", and "in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" we celebrate the Passover, with Christ feasting together with us according to the will of the lamb who says: "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life abiding in you"; "who takes away the sin of the world" and forbids the true destroyer (the destroyer not of Egypt alone, but of the whole human race) to touch us who celebrate the festival of the Passover with him. And we ascend, with the Lord himself established with us, from the lower places to the upper place, in which is the guest-chamber, which is shown by the understanding, which is in each man the householder, to the disciples of Christ. And let this upper house be great for us, that it may hold Jesus the Word of God and wisdom and truth and peace and everything that the Son of God is, who is not held except by those great in mind. And let this house be prepared by the householder, the understanding, for the Son of God, not only in an upper place nor only great but also cleansed, in no way having the filth of malice, as if gathered together and cast out by the brooms of the law. Let this house be also in the city of God, that is, in the Church. And let the ruler of that house not be one having his name known to just any people whatever: therefore also mystically Jesus says Go to a certain man, so that those who prepare the Passover for Christ may say to him: The Master says: At your house I will keep the Passover with my disciples, and let them also announce to that householder what he says: "The Master says: Where is the guest-chamber, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples", so that that householder who prepares the guest-chamber for Jesus and his disciples may show the upper place, both furnished and prepared and great, so that Jesus, coming thither, may keep the festival with his disciples.

But I think that the man who, as the disciples entered the city, met them "carrying a jar of water", whom Jesus willed that his disciples should follow as he went into the house, who was bringing that subtle water to the house, so that it might not only be cleansed, but also more fully washed with waters, was a certain one ministering to the householder (that is, to the understanding), carrying cleansing water in an earthen vessel, "that the sublimity of power may be of God", or certainly he was supplying drinkable water in that earthen vessel, so that the Son of God indeed might furnish the produce of the vine, but that understanding, the minister, might furnish out of the law and the prophets the water that is mingled with the wine of the Gospel word. We therefore who desire to be of the Church, wishing to celebrate the Passover with Jesus, let us follow that man who carries a vessel of water of this kind, whom I think to be Moses the giver of the law, carrying spiritual doctrine in corporal histories. But those who approach the law and the prophets as to the utterances of God himself, yet do not follow spiritually him who carries the vessel of living water, do not celebrate the Passover with Jesus nor drink the cup of the new testament. But let the disciples prepare the Passover for Jesus, and after the discourses of the disciples by which they have catechized the householder (that is, the understanding), let also the divinity of the Only-begotten come, feasting together with his disciples in the aforesaid house. Yet we ought to know that those who are in worldly feastings and cares do not ascend into that upper house, nor do they see its greatness nor consider the adornment of its furnishing; therefore neither do they celebrate the Passover with Jesus nor receive the bread of blessing from him nor the cup of the new testament.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

By the first day of the feast of unleavened bread, he means the day before that feast for they are accustomed always to reckon the day from the evening, and he makes mention of this in which in the evening the passover must be killed; for on the fifth day of the week they came unto Him.
