And this one calls the day before the feast of unleavened bread, speaking of the time when they came to Him, and another saith on this wise, "Then came the day of unleavened bread, when the passover must be killed;" by the word "came," meaning this, it was nigh, it was at the doors, making mention plainly of that evening. For they began with the evening, wherefore also each adds, when the passover was killed.

And they say, "Where wilt Thou that we prepare for Thee to eat the passover?" So even from this it is manifest, that He had no house, no place of sojourning; and I suppose neither had they. For surely they would have entreated him to come there. But neither had they any, having now parted with all things.

But wherefore did He keep the passover? To indicate by all things unto the last day, that He is not opposed to the law.
Commentary on Matthew

Now on the first day of the Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying: Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover? The first day of the Unleavened Bread is the fourteenth day of the first month, when the lamb is sacrificed and the moon is at its fullest and leaven is cast out. And among those disciples who came to the Lord asking: Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover, I reckon that Judas the betrayer was also present.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

And for what possible reason doth He send them to an unknown person? To show by this also that He might have avoided suffering. For He who prevailed over this man's mind, so that he received them, and that by words; what would He not have done with them that crucified Him, if it had been His will not to suffer? And what He did about the ass, this He did here also. For there too He saith, "If any man say aught unto you, ye shall say, that the Lord hath need of them;" and so likewise here, "The Master saith, I will keep the passover at thy house." But I marvel not at this only, that he received Him, being unknown, but that expecting to bring upon himself such enmity and implacable hostility, he despised the enmity of the multitude.

After this, because they knew him not, He gave them a sign, like as the prophet touching Saul, saying, "Thou shall find one going up and carrying a bottle;" and here, "carrying a pitcher." And see again the display of his power. For He did not only say, "I will keep the passover," but He adds another thing also, "My time is at hand." And this He did, at once continually reminding His disciples of the passion, so that exercised by the frequency of the prediction, they should be prepared for what was to take place; and at the same time to show to themselves, and to him that was receiving Him, and to all the Jews, which I have often mentioned, that not involuntarily doth He come to His passion. And He adds, "with my disciples," in order that both the preparation should be sufficient, and that the man should not suppose that He was concealing Himself.
Commentary on Matthew

But Jesus said: Go into the city to a certain man. The new Scripture keeps the custom of the Old Testament. We often read: So-and-so said to so-and-so; and: In such and such a place, which in Hebrew is called phelmoni and helmoni; and yet the name of the persons and of the places is not given. And you will find, he says, a certain man carrying a jar of water. Their names were passed over for this reason: that a free occasion for the festival might be opened to all who are going to keep the Passover.
Commentary on Matthew

And the disciples did as Jesus had appointed them, and they prepared the Passover. In another evangelist it is written that they found a large upper room, furnished and cleaned, and there they made ready for him. But it seems to me that the upper room is to be understood as the spiritual law, which, going out from the narrowness of the letter, receives the Savior in a lofty place, Paul saying this very thing: that the things which he formerly reckoned as gain he despised as refuse and rubbish, so that he might prepare a lodging worthy of the Lord.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 80

But when evening had come, he reclined at table with his disciples, and while they were eating he said: amen I say to you, that one of you will betray me.

While the disciples were eating the passover according to the commandment of the law, Jesus spoke — he who knew what was in man, and therefore had no need that anyone should give him testimony concerning man — and he spoke of Judas with the oath customary to him: amen I say to you, that one of you will betray me. For although he could from the outset have specifically pointed out the betrayer, this indeed he did not do, but said it generally, that one of you will betray me, so that by the testimony of the stricken heart the character of each one might be tested, so that he might both show the goodness of the disciples, in that they believed the words of Christ more than their own conscience, and the malice of Judas, in that he did not believe even him who knew his own counsels, so as to be troubled or made sad — granted that at first he supposed that he lay hidden, as though from a man — who, after he saw his own conscience … set within the very words of him, of which the first belonged to unbelief, but the second to shamelessness.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

"Now when the even was come, He sat down with the twelve disciples." Oh the shamelessness of Judas! For he too was present there, and came to partake both of the mysteries, and of the meal, and is convicted at the very table, when although he had been a wild beast, he would have become tame.

For this cause the evangelist also signifies, that while they are eating, Christ speaks of His betrayal, that both by the time and by the table he might show the wickedness of the traitor.
Commentary on Matthew
When evening had come, he reclined with the twelve disciples. Judas does everything so that suspicion of the betrayer may be removed.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

For when the disciples had done, as Jesus had appointed them, "when the even was come, He sat down with the twelve. And as they did eat, He said," we are told, "Verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me." And before the supper, He had even washed his feet. And see how He spares the traitor. For He said not, such a one shall betray me; but, "one of you," so as again to give him power of repentance by concealment. And He chooseth to alarm all, for the sake of saving this man. Of you, the twelve, saith He, that are everywhere present with me, whose feet I washed, to whom I promised so many things.
Commentary on Matthew

And as they were eating he said: Amen I say to you that one of you is going to betray me. He who had foretold his passion foretells the betrayer too, giving room for repentance, so that, when he understood that his thoughts and secret counsels were known, he might repent of his deed; and yet he does not point him out specifically, lest, being openly convicted, he should become more shameless. He casts the charge among the whole number, so that the one who is conscious of it may repent.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 81

And being exceedingly saddened they began each one to say: Is it I, Lord?.

But someone will ask: if the eleven apostles were of good conscience (since they were clean of any betrayal of their master), why were they saddened at the hearing of it, as though it could come to pass that one of them was he of whom it was spoken? But I judge that each of the disciples knew, from those things which Jesus had taught, that human nature is changeable and turnable to evil, and that in the struggle "against the principalities and powers and rulers of this world of darkness" it can come to pass that a man falls, either circumvented or having suffered force from the adversary powers to the accomplishing of evil. Considering this, therefore, each of the disciples, lest perhaps he himself were the one who had been foreknown as the betrayer, were saddened greatly, because it had been said to them: one of you will betray me, and they began to say, as though each one not knowing what was to be concerning himself: Is it I, Lord? And if it has reason that for this cause each of them, fearing, said: Is it I, Lord, then concerning all future things it must be feared by us who are weak, who have not yet received the wisdom of perfection, according to which the apostle says: "for I am confident that neither death nor life" and the rest "can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus". But he who is not yet perfect doubts concerning himself, as though he too could fall; according to which human weakness Paul, writing to the Corinthians, said: "but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself be made reprobate". And see: what he says, "lest perhaps, having preached to others, I myself be made reprobate", he so pronounces as one fearing, lest perhaps he too could both fall and become reprobate; but what he said, "I am confident" and the rest, is of a confident and firm man on account of his perfection, since a thousand contrary things have not the strength to separate him "from the love of Christ". But that the apostles were still weak and rightly feared is manifest from that which he says who knew the purpose of each one, that "you shall all suffer scandal in me in this night".

And that one who purposes better things is sometimes turned aside to malice, conquered in the struggle of the contrary powers, is manifest from that which is written concerning Peter: that he indeed, considering his own purpose, what disposition he had toward Christ, answered not with pretense but out of the truth of his heart (as far as concerned himself), that "if all shall be scandalized, I alone shall not be scandalized"; but the Savior, knowing that he would be weak in his promises, and that a man's brief fear was going to make him withdraw from the better purpose, said to him: "Amen I say to you that in this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me thrice". And to such as these it is not unfitting to say always: "do not glory in the Lord, for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth". And Paul likewise: "brothers", he says, "if a man be overtaken in any fault, you who are spiritual, strengthen such a one in the spirit of meekness, considering lest you too be tempted", teaching that our own outcome concerning ourselves is uncertain, although perhaps we hold the purpose of better things. But recalling all these things, that we do not know "what the coming day may bring forth" for us, we shall not be puffed up, nor be proud, nor ever glory, although we know that we have many good things; just as Paul also, when he had said concerning himself: "I am conscious of nothing in myself", adds besides: "but in this I am not justified", as one knowing that God sanctifies those whom he foreknows and calls "those whom he predestined".
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

Intolerable sorrow thereupon seized that holy company. And John indeed saith, they "were in doubt, and looked one upon another," and each of them asked in fear concerning himself, although conscious to themselves of no such thing. But this evangelist saith, that "being exceeding sorrowful, they began every one of them to say unto Him, Is it I, Lord?"

Mark at what time He discovered him. It was when it was His will to deliver the rest from this trouble, for they were even dead with the fear, wherefore also they were instant with their questions. But not only as desiring to deliver them from their distress He did this, but also as willing to amend the traitor. For since after having often heard it generally, he continued incorrigible, being past feeling, He being minded to make him feel more, takes off his mask.
Commentary on Matthew

And being greatly saddened they began each to say: Is it I, Lord? And surely the eleven apostles knew that they were planning nothing of the kind against the Lord; but they trust the master more than themselves, and, fearing their own frailty, they sorrowfully ask about a sin of which they had no consciousness.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 82

He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me.

Seeing them fearful about themselves, He pointed out the betrayer by the evidence of the prophetic voice that says: "he that eateth my bread with me hath magnified his supplanting against me"; for that saying does not differ from this which He says: he that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me. And this too is to be considered: what exactly the Savior meant to teach us when He gave His disciples a sign concerning Judas the betrayer from this, that he had put his own hand into the dish together with Jesus — into which (as I suppose) they dipped the flesh as they ate the Passover. But I suppose that He said this because He wished to make manifest the greatness of his malice, since the one whom He had received at the common table and who had eaten together with Him (perhaps because in the beginning he was acting well), this very man betrayed Jesus, who was embracing him with such great honors, and became mindful neither of the same salt nor of the table nor of the bread shared in common, but transgressing all those things for the promise of thirty coins he betrayed the bestower of such great goods. And this is truly the peculiar habit of exceedingly evil men, that after salt and bread they lie in wait for people — most of all when they have been harmed in nothing by those with whom they shared bread and salt. Finally, Daniel, prophesying thus concerning certain men of this deadly and utterly evil kind, said: "at one table they shall speak lies".

But if you can understand the spiritual table and the spiritual food and the Lord's supper, with all of which he had been made worthy by Christ, you will see more abundantly the multitude of his malice, in that he betrayed the Savior, his master and fellow-partaker of the divine table and cup (and this on the day of the Passover), remembering neither in bodily goods his master's love, nor in spiritual goods his teaching always shared without grudging. Such are all those in the Church who lie in wait for their brethren, with whom they have frequently been together at the same table of the body of Christ and at the same cup of His blood. But if we must also receive the interpretation of the dish itself, let us for our part abstain from things of this kind, lest we seem to say something frigid to certain people. Nevertheless, let him who wishes to find in this too something moral consider in the law, where gifts are offered by the princes of the several tribes at the dedication of the altar, and perhaps he will understand that there too the dish is to be understood as something: "on the first day", it says, "Nahshon the son of Amminadab, prince of the tribe of Judah, offered his gift. And he offered for his gift one silver dish, its weight a hundred and thirty, and one silver bowl of seventy shekels according to the holy shekel".
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

For when being sorrowful they began to say, "Is it I, Lord?" He answered and said, "He that dippeth with me in the dish, the same shall betray me."

Now some say that he was so bold as not to honor his Master, but to dip with Him: but to me Christ seems to have done this too, to shame him the more, and bring him over to a better disposition. For this act again has something more in it.

But these things we ought not to pass by at random, but they should be infixed in our minds, and wrath would find no place at any time.

For who, bearing in mind that supper, and the traitor sitting at meat with the Saviour of all, and Him who was to be betrayed thus meekly reasoning, would not put away all venom of wrath and anger? See at any rate how meekly He conducts Himself towards him.
Commentary on Matthew

But he answered and said: He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me. O the wonderful patience of the Lord! First he had said: One of you is going to betray me. The betrayer persists in evil; he reproves him more plainly, and yet he does not point out his name specifically. Judas, while the others were saddened and drew back their hands and forbade food to their mouths, with the same rashness and shamelessness with which he was going to betray him, even puts his hand into the dish with his master, so that by his boldness he might feign a good conscience.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 83

And the Son of Man indeed goes, as it is written of him; but woe to that man through whom the Son of Man shall be betrayed.

And Jesus indeed, according to what was seen, was going to suffer by the cross; but according to what he truly was, he was both going and remaining in the world with his disciples, guarding them in the faith. For they could not have remained in his faith, especially when they had seen him dead, unless their hearts had been invisibly guarded by him. And he did not say: woe to that man by whom he is betrayed but through whom he is betrayed, showing that there was another by whom he was being betrayed (that is, by the devil), while Judas himself was the minister of the betrayal. And woe not only to Judas, but to all betrayers of Christ; for whoever betrays the disciples of Christ, betrays Christ himself. Therefore they are indeed betrayed by the devil, yet through those men, and for this reason woe to them. For if the devil works all malice in men through men, then whoever is killed by someone, even if not by him yet through him has been killed. And if a judge shall have killed someone, unjustly bearing a sentence of death against someone, it must be known that he himself, by giving "place to the devil" in himself, offered himself as a minister to the devil for the killing of an innocent man. It were good for him, if that man had not been born, that is: for him it were good if he had not been born, because he had not been worthy even of this good, that he should be born. But since he had been fit, out of his own choice, that this ministry of betrayal should be accomplished through him, therefore he was born to his own harm, so that he might fall into the evil which according to his own purpose he deserved.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

"The Son of Man goeth, as it is written of Him, but woe to the man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed. It had been good for that man if he had not been born."

And these things again He said, both to restore the disciples, that they might not think the thing was a sign of weakness, and to amend the traitor.

"But woe unto that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born." See again in His rebukes His unspeakable meekness. For not even here with invective, but more in the way of compassion, doth He apply what He saith, but in a disguised way again.

But some one will say, Yet if it was written that He was to suffer these things, wherefore is Judas blamed, for he did the things that were written? But not with this intent, but from wickedness. For if thou inquire not concerning the motive, thou wilt deliver even the devil from the charges against him. But these things are not, they are not so. For both the one and the other are deserving of countless punishments, although the world was saved. For neither did the treason of Judas work out salvation for us, but the wisdom of Christ, and the good contrivance of His fair skill, using the wickednesses of others for our advantage.

"What then," one may say, "though Judas had not betrayed Him, would not another have betrayed Him?" And what has this to do with the question? "Because if Christ must needs be crucified, it must be by the means of some one, and if by some one, surely by such a person as this. But if all had been good, the dispensation in our behalf had been impeded." Not so. For the All wise knows how He shall bring about our benefits, even had this happened. For His wisdom is rich in contrivance, and incomprehensible. So for this reason, that no one might suppose that Judas had become a minister of the dispensation, He declares the wretchedness of the man.
Commentary on Matthew

The Son of Man indeed goes as it is written of him; but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man will be betrayed. Reproved neither the first time nor the second, he does not draw back his foot from the betrayal; rather, he feeds his shamelessness on the patience of the Lord and stores up for himself wrath on the day of wrath. Punishment is foretold, so that the torments announced might correct one whom shame had not overcome. But as to what follows:

It would have been good for him if that man had not been born, he is not on that account to be thought to have existed before he was born, on the ground that it can be well with no one except one who has existed; it is simply said that it is much better not to exist than to exist badly.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 84

But Judas answered and said: Is it I, Rabbi?

And observe that Judas, waiting through so long a discourse of Christ about himself, did not cut off His narrative with his own response, but after all the others he answered, saying Is it I, Rabbi? — not out of any desire to learn, but according to the custom of naming his teacher he called Him teacher, as if mocking Him, because He was called teacher when He was not worthy of that title. And Jesus said to him: You have said it, so that "out of his own mouth" He might judge him, since he had spoken as if in doubt: Is it I, Rabbi. Yet he was not in doubt according to his conscience, but pretended that he doubted about this. For he did not have that very fear which the rest of the apostles had; but he, without fear, spoke as though fearing. And therefore perhaps, after the individual questionings of all the apostles and after Christ's narrative concerning him, he too at last barely asked the question, as if from a certain calculation and cunning design, so that by questioning in a manner similar to the rest of the apostles he might for the time conceal the plan of his betrayal; for true and pressing sorrow does not endure delay, just as neither did that of the apostles endure it.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 81

But let us see what saith this wretched man, when convicted by his Master. What then saith he? "Is it I, Rabbi?" And why did he not ask this from the beginning? He thought to escape knowledge by its being said, "one of you;" but when He had made him manifest, he ventured again to ask, confiding in the clemency of his Master, that He would not convict him.

O blindness! Whereunto hath it led him? Such is covetousness, it renders men fools and senseless, yea reckless, and dogs instead of men, or rather even more fierce than dogs, and devils after being dogs. This man at least received unto him the devil even when plotting against him, but Jesus, even when doing him good, he betrayed, having already become a devil in will. For such doth the insatiable desire of gain make men, out of their mind, frenzy-smitten, altogether given up to gain, as was the case even with Judas.

And yet He might have said, O thou unholy, thou all unholy one; accursed, and profane; so long a time in travail with mischief, who hast gone thy way, and made satanical compacts, and hast agreed to receive money, and hast been convicted by me too, dost thou yet dare to ask? But none of these things did He say; but how? "Thou sayest." Fixing for us bounds and rules of long suffering.
Commentary on Matthew

And Judas, who betrayed him, answered and said: Is it I, rabbi? He said to him: You have said it. Because the others, sad and very sad, had asked: Is it I, Lord, lest he should seem to give himself away by keeping silent, he too, whom his conscience was gnawing, who had boldly put his hand into the dish, asks in the same way: Is it I, rabbi, and adds the feeling of one who flatters, or else a sign of unbelief. For the others, who were not going to betray him, say: Is it I, Lord; this one, who was going to betray him, calls him not lord but master, as if he would have an excuse if, having denied him as lord, he had at least betrayed a master. And he said to him: You have said it. The betrayer is refuted by the same reply with which he will afterwards answer Pilate.
The Didache, Chapters 9-10

Now concerning the Thanksgiving (Eucharist), thus give thanks. First, concerning the cup: We thank thee, our Father, for the holy vine of David Thy servant, which Thou madest known to us through Jesus Thy Servant; to Thee be the glory for ever. And concerning the broken bread: We thank Thee, our Father, for the life and knowledge which Thou modest known to us through Jesus Thy Servant; to Thee be the glory for ever. Even as this broken bread was scattered over the hills, and was gathered together and became one, so let Thy Church be gathered together from the ends of the earth into Thy kingdom; for Thine is the glory and the power through Jesus Christ for ever. But let no one eat or drink of your Thanksgiving (Eucharist), but they who have been baptized into the name of the Lord; for concerning this also the Lord hath said, Give not that which is holy to the dogs.

But after ye are filled, thus give thanks: We thank Thee, holy Father, for Thy holy name which Thou didst cause to tabernacle in our hearts, and for the knowledge and faith and immortality, which Thou modest known to us through Jesus Thy Servant; to Thee be the glory for ever. Thou, Master almighty, didst create all things for Thy name's sake; Thou gavest food and drink to men for enjoyment, that they might give thanks to Thee; but to us Thou didst freely give spiritual food and drink and life eternal through Thy Servant. Before all things we thank Thee that Thou art mighty; to Thee be the glory for ever. Remember, Lord, Thy Church, to deliver it from all evil and to make it perfect in Thy love, and gather it from the four winds, sanctified for Thy kingdom which Thou hast prepared for it; for Thine is the power and the glory for ever. Let grace come, and let this world pass away. Hosanna to the God (Son) of David! If any one is holy, let him come; if any one is not so, let him repent. Maran atha. Amen. But permit the prophets to make Thanksgiving as much as they desire.
On Prayer
Then we find, too, that His body is reckoned in bread: "This is my body." And so, in petitioning for "daily bread," we ask for perpetuity in Christ, and indivisibility from His body.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 86

Amen I say to you, that from now on I will not drink of this generation of the vine, until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.

But concerning the bread as well a similar thing is said in Luke: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you. I say to you that from now on I will not eat it, until it be fulfilled in the kingdom of God." Therefore the Savior will eat and drink that bread and paschal drink renewed "in the kingdom of God," and he will eat and drink with his disciples. For just as "he did not deem it robbery to be equal to God, but humbled himself even unto death," so he will eat the bread and drink of the generation of the vine, and he will drink it new, and by reason of his great goodness and his love of men he will eat and drink with his disciples, "when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father." For attend to what he says: when I shall drink it new with you, at no other time, except in the kingdom of my Father. And elsewhere, moreover, "the kingdom of God is not food and drink." For in a bodily sense, and according to the likeness of present food and drink, "the kingdom of God is not food and drink" … to those who have shown themselves worthy of the heavenly bread and the bread of angels and of that food of which the Savior says: "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work." But that "in the kingdom of God" we shall eat and drink, it is possible to demonstrate from many places of the Scriptures, especially from that which is written: "Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." Therefore this Passover will be fulfilled "in the kingdom of God," and Jesus will eat it with his disciples and will drink; and what the Apostle says, "Let no one judge you in food and in drink and the other things which are a shadow of things to come," has a revelation directed to the future mysteries concerning spiritual foods and drinks, of which the things that had been written in the Law concerning foods and drinks were a shadow. And it is manifest that we shall eat true food and drink true drink "in the kingdom of God," building up and strengthening through them that most true life.

And as for what he says, Jesus taking bread, and similarly taking the cup, let him who is indeed a little one "in Christ" and still carnal in Christ understand it in the common way; but let the more prudent one inquire, from whom Jesus, taking it. For it is God who gives, and he receives and gives to those who are worthy to receive from God the bread and the cup. But in what way God gives bread, Jacob too signifies when he says: "If the Lord my God shall be with me, and shall give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, of all things whatsoever thou, Lord, shalt give me, I will tithe a tenth to thee." Likewise it is written in the Gospel according to John: "Not Moses gave you bread, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven." And always Jesus, when these who together with him keep the feast are eating, taking bread from the Father gives thanks, and breaks it, and gives it to his disciples according to what each one of them is able to receive, and gives it saying: Take and eat, and shows, when he nourishes them with this bread, that it is his own body, since he himself is the Word, which we have need of both now and when it shall have been fulfilled "in the kingdom of God." But now indeed it is not yet fulfilled, but then it will be fulfilled, when we too shall have been prepared to receive the full Passover, which he came to fulfill, who came not "to loose the Law but to fulfill it," and now indeed to fulfill it "as through a glass in an enigma" of the fulfillment: "but then face to face" to fulfill it, "when that which is perfect shall have come."

If therefore we too wish to receive the bread of blessing from Jesus who is accustomed to give it, let us go "into the city" into the house of a certain man where Jesus makes "the Passover with" his "disciples," those known to him preparing it for him, and let us go up to the upper part of the house, "large and spread and prepared," where, taking the cup from the Father and giving thanks, he gives it to those who have gone up with him, saying: Drink, for this is my blood of the new testament. And it is both drunk and poured out: it is drunk indeed by the disciples. But it is poured out unto the remission of the sins committed by those by whom it is drunk and poured out. But if you ask, in what way it is also poured out, consider together with this word also that which is written: "Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts." But if the blood of the testament has been poured into our hearts unto the remission of our sins, when that drinkable blood has been poured out into our hearts, all the sins which we committed before are remitted and blotted out. But he himself who, having taken the cup, says: Drink of this, all of you, does not, when we drink, depart from us, but drinks it with us (since he himself is in each one), because we cannot, alone and without him, either eat of that bread or drink of the generation of the vine of that true vine. And do not wonder that he himself is both the bread and eats the bread with us, and he himself is also the drink of the generation of the vine and drinks with us. For the Word of God is almighty and is named by diverse appellations, and he himself is innumerable according to the multitude of his powers, since all power is one and himself.

Then he taught the disciples who had celebrated the feast with the Master and had received the bread of blessing and had eaten the body of the Word and had drunk the cup of thanksgiving, that for all these things they should say a hymn to the Father and pass from the height to the height, because the faithful man cannot at any time do anything in a low valley. For which reason they went up into the Mount of Olives, on which each olive tree, as a tree bearing fruit, can say: "But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God." And those who have not yet been made like a "fruitful olive tree in the house of God," but are still "like young olive shoots round about the table" of their spiritual Father, can be on the Mount of Olives, concerning which Zechariah also prophesies. And how fittingly the mount of mercy was chosen, where he was about to foretell the scandal of the weakness of his disciples: for he did not wish it to come to pass, but foretold what was to be, being even then prepared not to drive away the disciples as they departed, but to receive them as they turned back.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 85

But as they were eating, Jesus, taking bread and giving thanks, broke it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat, for this is my body. And taking the cup and giving thanks, he gave it to them, saying: Drink of this, all of you, for this is my blood of the new testament, which is poured out for many for the remission of sins.

This bread, which the God Word confesses to be his body, is the word that nourishes souls, the word proceeding from God the Word and the bread from the heavenly bread, which is set upon the table of which it is written: "You have prepared a table in my sight against those who trouble me". And this drink, which the God Word confesses to be his blood, is the word that gives drink and gloriously inebriates the hearts of those who drink, which is in the cup of which it is written: "And how glorious is your inebriating cup!" And this drink is the offspring of the true vine, which says: "I am the true vine", and it is the blood of that grape which, cast into the winepress of the passion, brought forth this drink; just as also the bread is the word of Christ made from that wheat which, "falling into the ground", "yielded much fruit". For the God Word was not calling that visible bread which he held in his hands his body, but the word in whose mystery that bread was to be broken. Nor was he calling that visible drink his blood, but the word in whose mystery that drink was to be poured out. For what else can the body of the God Word, or his blood, be, but the word that nourishes, and the word that "gladdens the heart"? But why did he not say: This is the bread of the new testament, as he said: This is the blood of the new testament? Because the bread is the word of righteousness by eating which souls are nourished, but the drink is the word of the knowledge of Christ according to the mystery of his birth and passion. Since, therefore, the testament of God has been established toward us in the blood of the passion of Christ, so that we, believing the Son of God to have been born and to have suffered according to the flesh, may be made saved — not in righteousness, in which alone, without faith in the passion of Christ, there could be no salvation — for this reason it was said only concerning the cup: This is the cup of the testament;
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 82

Ah! how great is the blindness of the traitor! Even partaking of the mysteries, he remained the same; and admitted to the most holy table, he changed not. And this Luke shows by saying, that after this Satan entered into him, not as despising the Lord's body, but thenceforth laughing to scorn the traitor's shamelessness. For indeed his sin became greater from both causes, as well in that he came to the mysteries with such a disposition, as that having approached them, he did not become better, either from fear, or from the benefit, or from the honor. But Christ forbad him not, although He knew all things, that thou mightest learn that He omits none of the things that pertain to correction. Wherefore both before this, and after this, He continually admonished him, and checked him, both by deeds, and by words; both by fear, and by kindness; both by threatening, and by honor. But none of these things withdrew him from that grievous pest.

Wherefore thenceforth He leaves him, and by the mysteries again reminds the disciples of His being slain, and in the midst of the meal His discourse is of the cross, by the continual repeating of the prediction, making His passion easy to receive. For if, when so many things had been done and foretold, they were troubled; if they had heard none of these things, what would they not have felt?

"And as they were eating, He took bread, and brake it." Why can it have been that He ordained this sacrament then, at the time of the passover? That thou mightest learn from everything, both that He is the lawgiver of the Old Testament, and that the things therein are foreshadowed because of these things. Therefore, I say, where the type is, there He puts the truth.

But the evening is a sure sign of the fullness of times, and that the things were now come to the very end.

And He gives thanks, to teach us how we ought to celebrate this sacrament, and to show that not unwillingly doth He come to the passion, and to teach us whatever we may suffer to bear it thankfully, thence also suggesting good hopes. For if the type was a deliverance from such bondage, how much more will the truth set free the world, and will He be delivered up for the benefit of our race. Wherefore, I would add, neither did He appoint the sacrament before this, but when henceforth the rites of the law were to cease. And thus the very chief of the feasts He brings to an end, removing them to another most awful table, and He saith, "Take, eat, This is my body, Which is broken for many."

And how were they not confounded at hearing this? Because He had before told unto them many and great things touching this.
Commentary on Matthew

And while they were dining, Jesus took bread and blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples and said: Take and eat, this is my body. And taking the cup he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying, and the rest. After the typical Passover had been fulfilled and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles, he takes bread, which strengthens the heart of man, and passes over to the true sacrament of the Passover, so that, just as Melchizedek, the priest of the most high God, had done in prefiguration of it when he offered bread and wine, he himself also might represent it in the truth of his own body and blood. In Luke we read of two cups with which he drank to the disciples, one of the first month and the other of the second, so that he who could not eat the lamb among the saints in the first month may eat the kid among the penitents in the second month.
SERMON 227

You hold the sacraments in their order. First, after the prayer, you are admonished to lift up your hearts; this befits the members of Christ. For if you have become members of Christ, where is your head? Members have a head. If the head had not gone before, the members would not follow. Where did our head go? What did you recite in the Creed? On the third day, He rose again from the dead, He ascended into heaven, He sits at the right hand of the Father. Therefore, our head is in Heaven. Thus when it is said: Lift up your hearts, you answer: We have them with the Lord. And so that you do not attribute the fact that you have your hearts with the Lord to your own strengths, merits, or labors—for it is a gift of God to have your heart lifted up to Him—the bishop or the priest who offers the sacrifice continues and says—when the people respond: We have them with the Lord—: Let us give thanks to the Lord our God, because we have our hearts with the Lord. Let us give thanks because if he did not give it, we would have our hearts on earth. And you attest by saying: It is right and just, that we should give thanks to Him who made us have our hearts lifted up to our head. Then, after the sanctification of God's sacrifice, because he willed that we ourselves should be his sacrifice—this was shown when the first sacrifice of God was laid down and we—meaning the sign of the reality—which we are; behold where the sanctification has been accomplished, we say the Lord's Prayer, which you have received and rendered. After it has been said: Peace be with you, and the Christians give each other a holy kiss. It is a sign of peace: as the lips show, let it be done in conscience, that is, just as your lips approach your brother's lips, let your heart not depart from his heart. Great indeed are the sacraments and very great indeed. Do you wish to know how they are commended? The Apostle says: Whosoever shall eat of the body of Christ or drink of the cup of the Lord unworthily, shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. What does it mean to receive unworthily? To receive it contemptuously, to receive it scoffingly. Do not make it seem cheap to you, because you see it. What you see passes away, but what is signified, the invisible, does not pass, but remains. Behold, it is received, eaten, consumed. Does the body of Christ perish? Does the Church of Christ perish? Do the members of Christ perish? By no means. Here they are cleansed, there they are crowned. Therefore, what is signified remains, even though that which signifies might seem to pass away.
A Treatise on the Soul

We may not, I say, we may not call into question the truth of the (poor vilified) senses, lest we should even in Christ Himself, bring doubt upon the truth of their sensation; lest perchance it should be said that He did not really "behold Satan as lightning fall from heaven; " that He did not really hear the Father's voice testifying of Himself; or that He was deceived in touching Peter's wife's mother; or that the fragrance of the ointment which He afterwards smelled was different from that which He accepted for His burial; and that the taste of the wine was different from that which He consecrated in memory of His blood. On this false principle it was that Marcion actually chose to believe that He was a phantom, denying to Him the reality of a perfect body.
On Modesty

For we now affirm: This is lawful to the Lord alone: may the power of His indulgence be operative at the present day! At those times, however, in which He lived on earth we lay this down definitively, that it is no prejudgment against us if pardon used to be conferred on sinners-even Jewish ones. For Christian discipline dates from the renewing of the Testament, and (as we have premised) from the redemption of flesh-that is, the Lord's passion.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 82

Wherefore that He establishes no more, for they had heard it sufficiently, but he speaks of the cause of His passion, namely, the taking away of sins. And He calls it blood of a New Testament, that of the undertaking, the promise, the new law. For this He undertook also of old, and this comprises the Testament that is in the new law. And like as the Old Testament had sheep and bullocks, so this has the Lord's blood. Hence also He shows that He is soon to die, wherefore also He made mention of a Testament, and He reminds them also of the former Testament, for that also was dedicated with blood. And again He tells the cause of His death, "which is shed for many for the remission of sins;" and He saith, "Do this in remembrance of me." Seest thou how He removes and draws them off from Jewish customs. For like as ye did that, He saith, in remembrance of the miracles in Egypt, so do this likewise in remembrance of me. That was shed for the preservation of the firstborn, this for the remission of the sins of the whole world. For, "This," saith He, "is my blood, which is shed for the remission of sins."

But this He said, indicating thereby, that His passion and His cross are a mystery, by this too again comforting His disciples. And like as Moses saith, "This shall be to you for an everlasting memorial," so He too, "in remembrance of me," until I come. Therefore also He saith, "With desire I have desired to eat this passover," that is, to deliver you the new rites, and to give a passover, by which I am to make you spiritual.

And He Himself drank of it. For lest on hearing this, they should say, What then? do we drink blood, and eat flesh? and then be perplexed (for when He began to discourse concerning these things, even at the very sayings many were offended), therefore lest they should be troubled then likewise, He first did this Himself, leading them to the calm participation of the mysteries. Therefore He Himself drank His own blood. What then must we observe that other ancient rite also? some one may say. By no means. For on this account He said, "Do this," that He might withdraw them from the other. For if this worketh remission of sins, as it surely doth work it, the other is now superfluous.

As then in the case of the Jews, so here also He hath bound up the memorial of the benefit with the mystery, by this again stopping the mouths of heretics. For when they say, Whence is it manifest that Christ was sacrificed? together with the other arguments we stop their mouths from the mysteries also. For if Jesus did not die, of what are the rites the symbols?

Seest thou how much diligence hath been used, that it should be ever borne in mind that He died for us? For since the Marcionists, and Valentinians, and Manichaeans were to arise, denying this dispensation, He continually reminds us of the passion even by the mysteries, (so that no man should be deceived); at once saving, and at the same time teaching by means of that sacred table. For this is the chief of the blessings; wherefore Paul also is in every way pressing this.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 7

The Savior had come into this world, that he might "offer his flesh as a victim to God for our sins". Before he offered this, amid the delays of the dispensations, he was drinking wine. In short, he was called "a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of publicans and sinners". But when the time of his cross arrived and "he was about to approach the altar" where he might immolate the victim of his flesh: "taking", it says, "the cup he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take, and drink of this". You, he says, "drink", who are not now about to approach the altar. But he himself, as one "about to approach the altar", says of himself: "Amen I say to you, that I will not drink of the generation of this vine, until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father". If any of you approaches with ears purified for hearing, let him gaze upon the secret of the ineffable mystery.… After these things, nevertheless, he will drink wine, but "new wine"; and "new wine" in "a new heaven and a new earth" and in "the new man" with "new men" and with those who "sing" to him "a new song". You see, therefore, that it is impossible for a new cup of the new vine to be drunk by him who is still "clothed with the old man with his acts". "For no one", he says, "puts new wine into old wineskins". If, then, you too wish to drink of this "new wine", be renewed and say: "even if our outer man is corrupted, yet he who is within is renewed from day to day".
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 82

Then, when He had delivered it, He saith, "I will not drink of the fruit of this wine, until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom." For because He had discoursed with them concerning passion and cross, He again introduces what He has to say of His resurrection, having made mention of a kingdom before them, and so calling His own resurrection.

And wherefore did He drink after He was risen again? Lest the grosser sort might suppose the resurrection was an appearance. For the common sort made this an infallible test of His having risen again. Wherefore also the apostles also persuading them concerning the resurrection say this, "We who did eat and drink with Him."

To show therefore that they should see Him manifestly risen, again, and that He should be with them once more, and that they themselves shall be witnesses to the things that are done, both by sight, and by act, He saith, "Until I drink it new with you," you bearing witness. For you shall see me risen again.

But what is "new." In a new, that is, a strange manner, not having a passible body, but now immortal and incorruptible, and not needing food.

It was not then for want that He both ate and drank after the resurrection, for neither did His body need these things any more, but for the full assurance of His resurrection.

And wherefore did He not drink water after He was risen again, but wine. To pluck up by the roots another wicked heresy. For since there are certain who use water in the mysteries; to show that both when He delivered the mysteries He had given wine, and that when He had risen and was setting before them a mere meal without mysteries, He used wine, "of the fruit," He saith, "of the vine." But a vine produces wine, not water.
Commentary on Matthew

But I say to you: I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father. He passes from carnal things to spiritual ones. That the vine transplanted from Egypt is the people of Israel, to whom the Lord speaks through Jeremiah: I planted you a true vine; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine, both Isaiah the prophet testifies, in the song which he sings to his beloved, and all Scripture here and there. The Lord therefore says that he will by no means drink of this vine except in the kingdom of his Father. The kingdom of the Father I take to be the faith of believers, the Apostle also confirming this very thing: The kingdom of God is within you. Therefore, when the Jews have received the kingdom of the Father (note that he says Father, not God: every name of Father refers to a son), when, I say, they have believed in God the Father and the Father has brought them to the Son, then the Lord will drink of their wine, and, in the likeness of Joseph reigning in Egypt, he will be made drunk with his brothers.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 82

"And when they had sung an hymn, they went out unto the Mount of Olives." Let them hear this, as many as, like swine eating at random, rudely spurn the natural table, and rise up in drunkenness, whereas it were meet to give thanks, and end with an hymn.

Hear this, as many as wait not again for the last prayer of the mysteries, for this is a symbol of that. He gave thanks before He gave it to His disciples, that we also may give thanks. He gave thanks, and sang an hymn after the giving, that we also may do this selfsame thing.

But for what reason doth He go forth unto the mountain? Making Himself manifest, that He may be taken, in order not to seem to hide himself. For He hastened to go to the place which was also known to Judas.
Commentary on Matthew

And when a hymn had been said, they went out to the Mount of Olives. This is what we read in a certain psalm: They have eaten and worshiped, all the fat ones of the earth. According to this example, whoever has been filled and made drunk with the bread and the cup of the Savior can praise the Lord and ascend the Mount of Olives, where there is refreshment from labors, solace for pain, and the knowledge of the true light.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 87

Then Jesus says to them: all of you will suffer scandal because of me this night; for it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered. But after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee (26, 31. 32).

Those who are made to stumble are not made to stumble in the day but in the night, and in that night in which Jesus is betrayed. For so too Peter, in denying, does not deny in the day but in the night, and in the night to which the light does not yet draw near; for he denies before the cock's crow. But if anyone should ask how, after so many and such great signs and wonders, and after words spoken from no lesser power (than that by which the signs and wonders had been done), the disciples are made to stumble, let him know that the discourse wishes to show through these things that, just as "no one can say the Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit", so no one can be without scandal apart from the Holy Spirit. But at the time when that was being fulfilled which Jesus had said: all of you will suffer scandal this night, "the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified". But we, after we have confessed the Lord Jesus in the Holy Spirit, since "those who are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God", if after the Holy Spirit we suffer scandal or deny, we will have no place of excuse, as though made to stumble without the Holy Spirit or denying without the Holy Spirit. And they indeed were made to stumble as still remaining in the night, but for us now "the night is far advanced, and the day has drawn near", on account of which "let us walk honorably as in the day". But he who walks honorably is in the light, and he who is in the light does not deny Christ, because he is not in the night. And furthermore, for this reason those men were made to stumble in the night (as the Lord himself testifies), because according to the Scripture, for us all, the Father "did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us" to the passion, so that for a little while the sheep of the flock, having suffered scandal, might be scattered, but after this be gathered together by Christ rising and going before them into Galilee — those who have wished to follow him into Galilee of the Gentiles, that "the people who were sitting in darkness may see a great light, and upon those who were sitting in the region and shadow of death may a light arise".
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 82

Then "He saith unto them, All ye shall be offended in me." After this He mentions also a prophecy, "For it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered abroad:" at once persuading them ever to give heed to the things that are written, and at same time making it plain that He was crucified, according to God's purpose; and by everything showing He was no alien from the old covenant, nor from the God preached therein, but that what is done is a dispensation, and that the prophets all proclaimed all things beforehand from the beginning that are comprised in the matter, so that they be quite confident about the better things also.

And He teaches us to know what the disciples were before the crucifixion, what after the crucifixion. For indeed they who, when He was crucified, were not able so much as to stand their ground, these after His death were mighty, and stronger than adamant.

And this self-same thing is a demonstration of His death, the fright and cowardice, I mean, of His disciples. For if when so many things have been both done and said, still some are shameless, and say that He was not crucified; if none of these things had come to pass, to what pitch of wickedness would they not have proceeded? So for this reason, not by His own sufferings only, but by what took place with respect to the disciples, He confirms the word concerning His death, and by the mysteries also, in every way confounding those that are diseased with the pest of Marcion. For this reason He suffers even the chief apostle to deny Him. But if He was not bound nor crucified, whence sprung the fear to Peter, and to the rest of the apostles.
Commentary on Zechariah

But I am amazed that some wish to thin out with allegorical interpretations this prophecy — which the evangelist Matthew referred to the Lord and Savior after the disciples fled at his passion, and says that it was then fulfilled —, and, while they want to seem to know more than the rest, do not hold to the rule of truth. For the evangelist Matthew relates: Then Jesus says to them: You will all take offense at me this night. For it is written: I will strike the shepherd and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered. And again: But all this was done that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples, leaving him, fled. Nor should it be thought that the testimony was taken from another place because in the Gospel God says that the shepherd was struck by himself, while in the present place we read that the sword and the point are commanded: Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.
Commentary on Matthew

Then Jesus says to them: All of you will suffer a stumbling block in me on this night. He foretells what they are going to suffer, so that, when they have suffered it, they may not despair of salvation, but may be set free by repenting. And he pointedly added: on this night you will suffer a stumbling block, because, just as those who get drunk get drunk at night, so also those who suffer a stumbling block undergo it in the night and in darkness. But let us say: The night has passed, and the day has drawn near.
Commentary on Matthew

For it is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered. This is written in other words in Zechariah the prophet, and, unless I am mistaken, it is said in the person of the prophet to God: Strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered, Psalm 68 (69) also, which is sung throughout in the Lord's person, agreeing with this sense: For they have persecuted him whom you have struck. And the good shepherd is struck so that he may lay down his life for his sheep, and that out of many flocks of errors there may be made one flock and one shepherd. Of this testimony more has been said in the little book which we wrote on the best kind of translating.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 20: ON THE SAVIOR'S PROMISE TO GO BEFORE THEM INTO GALILEE

When the Savior said that he was going to suffer and that he would rise again on the third day, he added, “And after I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee, there you will see me”; and likewise the angel said to the women (Matt. 26:32 and 28:7). — Yet he is found by the women and by his disciples in Jerusalem. To call the Savior’s words into question is unbelief; but I see that you are not doubting the Savior’s words, but seeking the meaning: why, since he was seen in Jerusalem after his Passion, did he say that he would be seen by them in Galilee. He was seen in Jerusalem, but only in part, to energize the spirits of the disciples; in Galilee, however, by all at once. Therefore, for those who were going to see him in Jerusalem in separate groups, he appointed Galilee so that he might appear to them all together, and there give commands for the ordering of their discipline.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 82

He suffers them not however, on the other hand, to wait until the sorrows, but what saith He? "But after I am risen again, I will go before you into Galilee." For not from Heaven doth He appear at once, neither will He depart into any distant country, but in the same nation, in which He had also been crucified, nearly in the same place, so as hereby again to assure them that He that was crucified was the very same that rose again, and in this way to comfort them more abundantly when in sorrow. Therefore also He said "in Galilee," that being freed from the fears of the Jews they might believe His saying. For which cause indeed He appeared there.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 88

But Peter answered and said to him: Even if all shall be made to stumble, I will never be made to stumble. And Jesus said to him: Amen I say to you, that on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. Peter says to him: Even if it should be for me to die with you, I will not deny you. And likewise all the disciples said the same.

The Apostle says in the epistle to the Romans: "But let God be true, and every man a liar, as it is written" — not commanding that every man become a liar, but declaring that he is a liar, from the Psalm which says: "I said in the excess of my mind: every man is a liar". But here Peter, hearing the Savior say "you shall all suffer stumbling in me this night", was professing to make our Lord a liar through those words which, confident in himself, he spoke: if all shall be made to stumble, I will not be made to stumble, not considering that he who said: "I am the truth" could not lie. On this account (as I judge) all the disciples indeed were made to stumble only in Jesus, but Peter, who supposed that the truth could be made a liar, was not only made to stumble, but was even abandoned on account of his bold promise, and, alongside his stumbling, he also denied.

And because he spoke not only inconsiderately but almost impiously: even if all shall be made to stumble in you, I will not be made to stumble, and, not reflecting on the slippery nature of humanity, uttered a great word, therefore he was not abandoned only for a little, so that even if he denied, he would deny but once. But he is abandoned more abundantly, so that he denied three times, that the boldness of his promise might be exposed — through a single maidservant both asking him this very thing and saying: "you too were with Jesus the Galilean" …, and he denied "before all, saying: I do not know what you are saying", and again he denied not simply but "with an oath", and a third time not only with an oath but with a curse: "for I do not know the man". And through this we are instructed never to promise anything without reflection concerning our human condition, as though we were able to fulfill the confession of Christ from ourselves, or anything of God's precepts, since the Apostle admonishes us and says: "do not be high-minded, but fear". For he ought, after he heard "you shall all suffer stumbling this night", to have entreated the Lord and said: even if all shall be made to stumble in you, be in me, that I be not made to stumble; and: grant me especially this grace, that at the time when all your disciples shall have suffered stumbling, I may not fall into denial nor be made to stumble from the beginning. For if he had entreated, perhaps, once the maidservants and the other servants had been removed from him, he would not have denied; for it could not come to pass that, when the questioning had been made, he could have said "the Lord Jesus" "in the Holy Spirit" or have confessed, since "the Holy Spirit had not yet been given".

But you will ask whether it was possible that he should not even once be made to stumble, since the Savior says: "you shall all suffer stumbling in me". To which question someone will answer that it was necessary, since a most truthful mouth foretold that "all of you" will be made to stumble, that what had been foretold by Jesus should come to pass. But another will say that he who, entreated by the Ninevites, did not do what he had foretold through Jonah (on account of the repentance of the Ninevites), to him it was possible to repel the stumbling even from Peter, had he entreated him. But as it is, his bold promise, made indeed from a ready but not prudent disposition, became for him the cause not only that he was made to stumble but that he even denied three times. You will ask further, whether, after he heard Jesus saying: amen I say to you, before the cock crows on this night, you will deny me three times, if he had not added: even if it should be for me to die with you, I will not deny you, but had instead entreated that the denial foreknown of him be repelled from him, whether perhaps he would not have denied. And someone indeed says that Peter's entreaty had room, when he had said: "you shall all suffer stumbling in me", to receive help so that he might not be made to stumble; for it had not been said with an "amen": "you shall all suffer stumbling". But after he pronounced it with the affirmation of an oath, it was not possible that he should not deny. For if Christ's amen was an oath, he would have lied in saying: amen I say to you, if Peter had spoken the truth that I will not deny you.

But the rest of the disciples of Jesus seem to me, with foresight and reflection (in that it had first been said "you shall all suffer stumbling in me this night"), to have said nothing and made no profession as though they were not to be made to stumble; for they saw that Jesus was truthful in foretelling these things. But to this which was said to Peter alone, amen I say to you, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times, they promised likewise with Peter: even if it should be for us to die with you, we will not deny you. This Peter indeed did unfittingly, after Christ's prophecy concerning him that he would deny three times before the cock's crowing; but the rest, as those who were not included in that prophecy nor held bound in the things which had been said to Peter, answered with a promise, not desiring by their promises to make the Lord a liar, as Peter wished to do. For just as, when he had been transfigured on the high mountain, when Moses and Elijah appeared in glory together with Jesus, he said: "do you wish that we make here three tabernacles, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah? not knowing what he was saying", (as the Scripture testifies concerning him), so also here, "not knowing what he was saying", he said: even if it should be for me to die with you, I will not deny you. For to die with Jesus, who was dying for us all, that we might live, did not belong to men, since all had been in sins and all had need that another should die for them, not they themselves for others.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 82

"But Peter answered and said, Though all men should be offended because of Thee, yet will I never be offended."

What sayest thou, O Peter? the prophet said, "The sheep shall be scattered;" Christ hath confirmed the saying, and sayest thou, No? Is not what passed before enough, when Thou saidst, "Far be it from Thee," and thy mouth was stopped? For this then He suffers him to fall, teaching him thereby to believe Christ in all things, and to account His declaration more trustworthy than one's own conscience. And the rest too reaped no small benefit from his denial, having come to know man's weakness, and God's truth. For when He foretells anything, we must no longer be subtle, nor lift up ourselves above the common sort. For, "thy rejoicing," it is said, "thou shall have in thyself, and not in another." For where he should have prayed, and have said, Help us, that we be not cut off, he is confident in himself, and saith, "Though all men should be offended in Thee, yet will I never;" though all should undergo this, I shall not undergo it, which led him on by little and little to self-confidence. Christ then, out of a desire to put down this, permitted his denial. For since he neither submitted to Him nor the prophet (and yet for this intent He brought in the prophet besides, that they may not gainsay), but nevertheless since he submitted not to His words, he is instructed by deeds.

And He said sharply reproving him, and showing that his fall was more grievous than the rest, and needed more help. For the matters of blame were two; both that he gainsaid; and, that he set himself before the other; or rather a third too, namely, that he attributed all to himself.

To cure these things then, He suffered the fall to take place, and for this cause also leaves the others, and addresses Himself earnestly to him. For, "Simon," saith He, "Simon, behold Satan hath desired to have you that he may sift you as wheat;" that is, that he may trouble, confound, tempt you; but "I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not."

And why, if Satan desired all, did He not say concerning all, I have prayed for you? Is it not quite plain that it is this, which I have mentioned before, that it is as reproving him, and showing that his fall was more grievous than the rest, that He directs His words to him?

And wherefore said He not, But I did not suffer it, rather than, "I have prayed?" He speaks from this time lowly things, on His way to His passion, that He may show His humanity. For He that has built His church upon Peter's confession, and has so fortified it, that ten thousand dangers and deaths are not to prevail over it; He that hath given him the keys of Heaven, and hath put him in possession of so much authority, and in no manner needed a prayer for these ends (for neither did He say, I have prayed, but with His own authority, "I will build my church, and I will give thee the keys of Heaven"), how should He need to pray, that He might brace up the shaken soul of a single man? Wherefore then did He speak in this way? For the cause which I mentioned, and because of their weakness, for they had not as yet the becoming view of Him.

How then was it that He denied? he said not, that thou mayest not deny, but that thy faith fail not, that thou perish not utterly. For this came from His care.

For indeed fear had driven out all else, for it was beyond measure, and it became beyond measure, since God had to an exceeding degree deprived him of His help, and He did exceedingly deprive him thereof, because there was to an exceeding degree in him the passion of self-will and contradiction. In order then that He might pluck it up by the roots, therefore He suffered the terror to overtake him.

For in proof that this passion was grievous in him, he was not content with his former words, gainsaying both prophet and Christ, but also after these things when Christ had said unto him, "Verily I say unto thee, that this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice," he replieth, "Though I should die with Thee, I will not deny Thee in any wise." And Luke signifies moreover, that the more Christ warned him, so much the more did Peter exceedingly oppose Him.

What mean these things, O Peter? When He was saying, "One of you shall betray me," thou didst fear lest thou shouldest be the traitor, and didst constrain the disciple to ask, although conscious to thyself of no such thing; but now, when He is plainly crying out, and saying, "All shall be offended," art thou gainsaying it, and not once only, but twice and often? For this is what Luke saith.

Whence then did this come to him? From much love, from much pleasure. I mean, that after that he was delivered from that distressing fear about the betrayal, and knew the traitor, he then spoke confidently, and lifted himself up over the rest, saying, "Though all men shall be offended, yet will I not be offended." And in some degree too his conduct sprung from jealousy, for at supper they reasoned "which of them is the greater," to such a degree did this passion trouble them. Therefore He checked him, not compelling him to the denial, God forbid! but leaving him destitute of His help, and convicting human nature.

See at any rate after these things how he was subdued. For after the resurrection, when he had said, "And what shall this man do?" and was silenced, he ventured no more to gainsay as here, but held his peace. Again, towards the assumption, when he heard, "It is not for you to know times or seasons," again he holds his peace, and contradicts not. After these things, on the house, and by the sheet, when he heard a voice saying to him, "What God hath cleansed, call not thou common," even though he knew not for the time what the saying could be, he is quiet, and strives not.

All these things did that fall effect, and whereas before that he attributes all to himself, saying, "Though all men shall be offended, yet will I not be offended;" and, "If I should die, I will not deny Thee" (when he should have said, If I receive the assistance from Thee); yet after these things altogether the contrary, "Why do ye give heed to us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made him to walk?"

Hence we learn a great doctrine, that a man's willingness is not sufficient, unless any one receive the succor from above; and that again we shall gain nothing by the succor from above, if there be not a willingness. And both these things do Judas and Peter show; for the one, though he had received much help, was profited nothing, because he was not willing, neither contributed his part; but this one, though he was ready in mind, because he received no assistance, fell. For indeed of these two things is virtue's web woven.

Wherefore I entreat you neither (when you have cast all upon God) to sleep yourselves, nor, when laboring earnestly, to think to accomplish all by your own toils. For neither is it God's will that we should be supine ourselves, therefore He worketh it not all Himself; nor yet boasters, therefore He did not give all to us; but having removed what was hurtful in either way, left that which is useful for us. Therefore He suffered even the chief apostle to fall, both rendering him more humbled in mind, and training him thenceforth to greater love. "For to whom more is forgiven," it is said, "he loveth more."

Let us then in everything believe God, and gainsay Him in nothing, though what is said seem to be contrary to our thoughts and senses, but let His word be of higher authority than both reasonings and sight. Thus let us do in the mysteries also, not looking at the things set before us, but keeping in mind His sayings.

For His word cannot deceive, but our senses are easily beguiled. That hath never failed, but this in most things goeth wrong. Since then the word saith, "This is my body," let us both be persuaded and believe, and look at it with the eyes of the mind.
Commentary on Matthew

But Peter answered and said to him: Even if all are scandalized, I will never be scandalized. It is not rashness, nor is it a lie; it is the faith of the apostle Peter and his burning affection toward the Lord Savior, of which we spoke above.
Commentary on Matthew

Jesus said to him: Amen I say to you that on this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. Peter made his promise out of the ardor of faith, and the Savior, as God, knew what was to come. And note that Peter denies in the night, and denies a third time; but after the cock crowed and, as the darkness waned, the approaching light was announced, he turned and wept bitterly, washing away the filth of the denial with tears.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 89

Then Jesus came with them to an estate called Gethsemane.

To one who knows the interpretation of Hebrew names, even the name of this estate which is called Gethsemane is of use for making this place clear, since it is not without reason that the name of the estate too is set down in Matthew and in Mark. But we, passing that over, suggest only this: how Jesus came with his disciples to this estate which is called Gethsemane, taking them out of that place in which he had eaten the Passover with them. For it was not fitting that, when he was being betrayed, he should be seized from that place where he had eaten the Passover with the disciples. But it was fitting also that, before he was betrayed, he should pray and, for praying, should choose a clean place for the prayer; for he knew that, just as air differs from purer air, so does the earth of a holy place differ from that of a holier one, as it is written: "the place in which you stand is holy ground". And you will ask whether, besides the disposition of the one praying, the prayer also becomes cleaner and more acceptable from the place of prayer in which one prays, according to what is written: "my house shall be called a house of prayer", concerning which it is also said elsewhere: "and he heard my voice from his holy temple". And a man of the Jews indeed does not even doubt about such a thing; but he who, because of the teaching of Christ, has withdrawn from "Jewish fables" and from all things that are understood by them in a bodily way, will say that a prayer does not become different from another prayer on account of the place, but rather because it is better to pray with no one than to pray with wicked men. And for the demonstration of this tradition he will use the example that Jesus, in the house of Jairus the priest, being about to pray for his dead daughter, "cast them all outside" and chose only three with him, who had also on the mountain been made witnesses of his transfiguration. For on account of this, in the churches of Christ too, such a custom has held, that those who are manifest in great offenses are cast out from the common prayer, lest a "little leaven" that is not "from a clean heart" of those praying corrupt the whole lump of unity and of concord.

But this meaning also has something that may justly be objected to those who do not understand as they ought, taking occasion to say to their neighbor: "do not draw near to me, for I am clean". Which the Pharisee also did toward the publican who stood far off and beat his breast and said: "Lord, be merciful to me a sinner". Therefore we ought to do this with measure, so that we neither pray with the unworthy for the honor of prayer (according to him who said: "if two of you agree together upon one thing, concerning whatever they ask, it shall be done for them"), nor despise our inferiors, setting ourselves before them through the lapse of boasting (according to him who said: "he who exalts himself shall be humbled"). And these things we have treated on account of what was said: sit here, while I go over there to pray.
Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83

Because they clung to Him inseparably, therefore He saith, "Tarry ye here, while I go away and pray." For it was usual with Him to pray apart from them. And this He did teaching us in our prayers, to prepare silence for ourselves and great retirement.
Commentary on Matthew

Then Jesus came with them to an estate which is called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples: Sit here while I go over there and pray. Gethsemane is interpreted most fertile valley; there he ordered the disciples to sit for a little while and to wait for his return, while the Lord alone prayed for all.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 90

And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and heavy, or as Mark explains it, "he began to be afraid and heavy". Now these same disciples he had also taken up onto the mountain when he was to be transfigured, and to the daughter of Jairus the priest. And I ask whether perhaps he saw something more secret, in the time before he suffered, when Jesus, going to that place, wished to pray. For perhaps he saw standing near him "the kings of the earth and the princes" gathered "together against the Lord and against" him, "his Christ". And on this account, as though those many were set against him and mighty in wickedness, he began to be sorrowful and heavy, or even "to be afraid". And consider that he did not say: he was sorrowful and heavy, but: he began to be sorrowful and heavy. For there is a great difference between being sorrowful and beginning to be sorrowful.
